blocks.text: Unlock Claude's Potential

You've likely used AI to speed up tasks and improve results. Yet, there's always more of what you can unlock — and Claude is built exactly for that. So, in this course, you'll learn about the features that most people never touch. Eager to level up your AI skills? Let's dive in!
What Connectors Do
When you start a work conversation in a blank chat, you often need to provide context before Claude can help. Connectors remove that step entirely.
Imagine having a couple of tables in Google Sheets that you need to compare with each other and write a report based on that. Normally, you'll need to:

1. Download the tables first.
  2. Insert them into the chat with Claude.
  3. Describe the context of what these tables mean.
  4. Prompt it to analyze and compare them.
  5. Ask it to write a report based on the results.
  6. Transfer the report to Google Docs by yourself.
With Connectors, you would only need to connect Claude to your Google Workspace and prompt it to do the work. That's it!
Understanding Connectors

Connectors link Claude directly to the tools where your work already lives — Gmail, Google Drive, Notion, Asana, Slack, and others. 

As a result, instead of gathering materials and pasting them in, you can just describe what you need, and Claude will retrieve it from the source and do the necessary work.
Connectors are useful across many tools and workflows. They make the biggest difference when:

• Source material is spread out: e.g., a project brief in Notion, updates in Slack, and files in Drive, all needed for one task
  • You need the latest version: e.g., live sales data from Sheets, not a copy from last week
  • Context is too large to paste: e.g., a full Gmail thread that would take forever to copy manually
In each of these contexts, you can connect your workspaces to Claude and ask it to do whatever you need with the data stored there.
Setting the Connectors Up

To set the Connectors up, open the "+" menu in chat, go to Add connectors → Browse connectors, choose the tool you want, and complete the authorization flow. Claude then uses that connection only within the scope of the permissions you granted.

Connectors differ in what they're allowed to do.
  • Read-focused connectors, such as Google Gmail, let Claude search for and retrieve content.
  • Write-mode connectors, like Asana and Slack, go further: Claude can create tasks, update project status, or draft messages that you review before anything is sent.
Check each connector's page in the Connectors Directory to see which actions it supports before you authorize it.
blocks.title: One Thing to Know Before You Connect Anything

blocks.text: Not Everything Should Be on Autopilot
Write-mode connectors open up real possibilities, but they also raise a question read-mode never does: what should Claude be allowed to do without checking with you first?
A useful way to think about it is three tiers:

• Delegate freely: retrieval, summarization, drafting things you'll review anyway.
  • Requires your approval: anything that creates, sends, or changes something other people will see.
  • Never delegate: irreversible actions, sensitive data access, anything where a mistake is hard to walk back.

feedbackCorrect.text: Anything that creates, sends, or visibly changes something for other people belongs in the approval tier. Summarization stays in your chat with Claude — no one else sees it unless you share it. The other three actions all leave a trace that someone else will react to.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Summarizing a Slack channel is internal to your conversation with Claude — it doesn't create anything other people will see or react to. The other three options do, which is what puts them in the approval tier.

options.label: Creating a new Asana task and assigning it to a teammate
Sending a reply on your behalf
Summarizing the last week of a Slack channel
Updating a project's status from "in progress" to "complete"

blocks.question: Your Claude now has access to Gmail, Asana, Drive, and Slack. Which actions should require your explicit approval before Claude executes them?

blocks.text: A Scenario to Work Through
To go through the full flow, let's now look at this situation:

• You're two weeks out from a product launch.
  • Planning documents are spread across Drive.
  • Stakeholder questions are buried in email threads.
  • Your project board has tasks you're not certain are actually closed.
Before you can make decisions, you need a clear picture of what's ready and what isn't.
First, you need to connect to Gmail or Google Drive. To do this, once you go to the Connectors space, select the connector you want and complete the authorization flow.

Next, you need a good prompt to ask Claude to retrieve information and produce something you can act on.

That second layer — the analytical instruction on top of retrieval — is what separates a useful output from a well-organized list of documents.

blocks.exampleResponse: Finalized: Messaging guide and pricing page — no action needed. Needs a decision: — Legal sign-off doc has one unresolved clause — flagged for review before launch. — Two onboarding docs conflict on trial period length: one says 14 days, the other 30. These need to be reconciled before any customer-facing materials go live. No issues found: Product roadmap, launch checklist, and press release draft are consistent and up to date. Three items require a decision before you go live: the legal clause, and the onboarding conflict.
blocks.prompt: Fill in the gaps to see how you can build a Google Drive connector prompt.
blocks.template:
Search Google Drive for [document type] related to our upcoming launch. Focus on files updated in the last [time frame].
Don't just summarize — [reasoning instruction] across documents, and flag anything that requires a decision before we go live.

blocks.text:
See how that worked?

A summary prompt would have returned a tidy list of what each document contains. 

In turn, the reasoning instruction — find contradictions, flag decisions — is what surfaced the onboarding conflict and the unresolved legal clause.

Every effective connector prompt has two layers: what to pull, and what to do with it. Skip the second layer, and you get an organized list — useful, but nothing Claude couldn't have done from a paste. The reasoning instruction is what turns retrieval into analysis.
  • Name the source precisely: which tool (if you use more than one connector), folder, label, or project
  • Add the analytical task: what Claude should find, compare, or flag in what it retrieves
  • Specify the output format: a structured brief, a prioritized list, a risk summary
blocks.title: 💡 Retrieval Is the Setup, Reasoning Is the Work

blocks.text: When the Context Isn't in One Tool
You've found contradictions within the documents from Google Drive. However, the whole context still lives across several tools:

• Launch status lives in Drive
  • Stakeholder questions are in Gmail
  • Overdue tasks are in Asana
Pulling from each separately and piecing the picture together yourself puts the synthesis work back on you. Connectors exist exactly to remove that burden.

For a prompt that draws on multiple sources in a single pass, all connectors must be active within the same conversation. Connect each one through the "+" menu before you start. Once all three appear as active, a single prompt can reach all of them simultaneously.

blocks.exampleResponse: Launch Readiness Brief On track: pricing finalized, legal reviewed (one clause outstanding), 13/17 Asana tasks complete. Needs action: conflicting onboarding docs (Drive), unanswered stakeholder pricing question (Gmail, 5 days old), 3 overdue QA tasks (Asana). Critical this week: QA sign-off, onboarding conflict, stakeholder response.
blocks.prompt: Complete this three-connector prompt. You're pulling from Drive, Gmail, and Asana to build a single launch-readiness picture.
blocks.template:
Pull [document type] from Google Drive updated in the last two weeks.
Scan Gmail for [email scope] under our launch label.
Check Asana for tasks [project name] project that are overdue or flagged as at risk.
Synthesize into a structured brief that separates what's on track from [category], and lists the three most critical items to resolve this week.

blocks.text: Great Job!

The brief identified three things that need to move this week and listed critical items to resolve.

That's how Connectors can increase your efficiency by finding the need-to-focus areas with just one prompt!
When Connectors Use the Wrong Sources
The launch brief you just got back looked clean and confident. But connectors can return outputs that look just as confident, even when built on the wrong inputs.
Connectors fail in four predictable ways:

• Stale data: The retrieval missed recent updates, and Claude doesn't flag it.
  • Permission gaps: Claude was blocked from a folder or thread it needed access to, and the output reflects only what it could see.
  • Too much context: Claude retrieved everything technically relevant, and the actual signal got buried.
  • File structure misreads: Claude pulled from the wrong tab, the template instead of the live doc, or an outdated version.
You only catch them by checking the inputs against what Claude reported.

Imagine you ask Claude to pull the pricing for an upcoming client proposal from your Drive's pricing folder.

Claude returns a clean breakdown. You drop them into the proposal and send it.

A day later, your sales lead flags that the numbers are 6 months out of date. The current pricing lives in a different file in the same folder.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! When a folder contains multiple files that match the prompt, Claude has to pick one, and without explicit instruction, it might pick a reasonable-looking, but wrong one. The fix is naming the exact source.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. Time scope isn't the issue, as both files exist right now. The Drive connector reads pricing fine; it's not a tool limitation. And Claude wasn't asked to compare versions, so reasoning didn't fail. Claude chose the wrong file from a folder of similar-looking options before reasoning ever started. The fix is naming the exact source.

options.label: The retrieval was scoped to a time window that excluded the current file
The Drive connector doesn't reliably read pricing data
Claude's reasoning failed to compare the two versions
Claude picked one of several matching files without knowing which was current

blocks.question: What is the most likely reason Claude pulled from the archived file instead of the current one?

blocks.text:
Each input failure mode has a specific fix:
  • Stale data → tighten the time scope or name the exact filter
  • Permission gaps → check what Claude actually has access to before re-prompting
  • Too much context → narrow the source to a specific folder, label, or project
  • File structure misreads → name the exact tab, version, or sub-document
If the inputs were right and the output is still off, then it's a reasoning problem.

blocks.title: 💡 Connectors for Breadth, Manual Upload for Depth

blocks.text: The Pattern Behind Any Connector Workflow
The scenario in this lesson used launch readiness, but the same structure can apply to various workflows:

• A client review
  • A hiring decision
  • A quarterly planning session
  • Or any situation where context is scattered across tools and needs to be synthesized into something actionable
Connect what the task requires, pair retrieval with a reasoning instruction, and let the output drive what happens next.

• Connectors pull live data from your tools. No more manual context gathering.
  • Good connector prompts have two layers: what to pull and what to do with it.
  • Multi-connector prompts enable cross-source insights. They help Claude synthesize related context from multiple sources.
  • Connectors aren't always best. Use uploads for focused, single-document analysis.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

You can now pull live context from across your tools in a single prompt, write retrieval and reasoning prompts, spot the ways connectors quietly fail, and tell when a connector beats a manual upload. In the next lesson, you'll push Claude's reasoning further with Thinking and Research — the modes that turn quick answers into deep, structured analysis. Together with Connectors, they make Claude useful for the work you've been putting off because it was too big to tackle on your own. Let's keep going!

feedbackIncorrect.text: Summarizing a Slack channel is internal to your conversation with Claude — it doesn't create anything other people will see or react to. The other three options do, which is what puts them in the approval tier.

options.label: Creating a new Asana task and assigning it to a teammate
Sending a reply on your behalf
Summarizing the last week of a Slack channel
Updating a project's status from "in progress" to "complete"

blocks.question: Your Claude now has access to Gmail, Asana, Drive, and Slack. Which actions should require your explicit approval before Claude executes them?

blocks.text: A Scenario to Work Through
To go through the full flow, let's now look at this situation:

• You're two weeks out from a product launch.
  • Planning documents are spread across Drive.
  • Stakeholder questions are buried in email threads.
  • Your project board has tasks you're not certain are actually closed.
Before you can make decisions, you need a clear picture of what's ready and what isn't.
First, you need to connect to Gmail or Google Drive. To do this, once you go to the Connectors space, select the connector you want and complete the authorization flow.

Next, you need a good prompt to ask Claude to retrieve information and produce something you can act on.

That second layer — the analytical instruction on top of retrieval — is what separates a useful output from a well-organized list of documents.

blocks.exampleResponse: Finalized: Messaging guide and pricing page — no action needed. Needs a decision: — Legal sign-off doc has one unresolved clause — flagged for review before launch. — Two onboarding docs conflict on trial period length: one says 14 days, the other 30. These need to be reconciled before any customer-facing materials go live. No issues found: Product roadmap, launch checklist, and press release draft are consistent and up to date. Three items require a decision before you go live: the legal clause, and the onboarding conflict.
blocks.prompt: Fill in the gaps to see how you can build a Google Drive connector prompt.
blocks.template:
Search Google Drive for [document type] related to our upcoming launch. Focus on files updated in the last [time frame].
Don't just summarize — [reasoning instruction] across documents, and flag anything that requires a decision before we go live.

blocks.text:
See how that worked?

A summary prompt would have returned a tidy list of what each document contains. 

In turn, the reasoning instruction — find contradictions, flag decisions — is what surfaced the onboarding conflict and the unresolved legal clause.

Every effective connector prompt has two layers: what to pull, and what to do with it. Skip the second layer, and you get an organized list — useful, but nothing Claude couldn't have done from a paste. The reasoning instruction is what turns retrieval into analysis.
  • Name the source precisely: which tool (if you use more than one connector), folder, label, or project
  • Add the analytical task: what Claude should find, compare, or flag in what it retrieves
  • Specify the output format: a structured brief, a prioritized list, a risk summary
blocks.title: 💡 Retrieval Is the Setup, Reasoning Is the Work

screens.title: 💡 Retrieval Is the Setup, Reasoning Is the Work

blocks.text: When the Context Isn't in One Tool
You've found contradictions within the documents from Google Drive. However, the whole context still lives across several tools:

• Launch status lives in Drive
  • Stakeholder questions are in Gmail
  • Overdue tasks are in Asana
Pulling from each separately and piecing the picture together yourself puts the synthesis work back on you. Connectors exist exactly to remove that burden.

For a prompt that draws on multiple sources in a single pass, all connectors must be active within the same conversation. Connect each one through the "+" menu before you start. Once all three appear as active, a single prompt can reach all of them simultaneously.

blocks.exampleResponse: Launch Readiness Brief On track: pricing finalized, legal reviewed (one clause outstanding), 13/17 Asana tasks complete. Needs action: conflicting onboarding docs (Drive), unanswered stakeholder pricing question (Gmail, 5 days old), 3 overdue QA tasks (Asana). Critical this week: QA sign-off, onboarding conflict, stakeholder response.
blocks.prompt: Complete this three-connector prompt. You're pulling from Drive, Gmail, and Asana to build a single launch-readiness picture.
blocks.template:
Pull [document type] from Google Drive updated in the last two weeks.
Scan Gmail for [email scope] under our launch label.
Check Asana for tasks [project name] project that are overdue or flagged as at risk.
Synthesize into a structured brief that separates what's on track from [category], and lists the three most critical items to resolve this week.

blocks.text: Great Job!

The brief identified three things that need to move this week and listed critical items to resolve.

That's how Connectors can increase your efficiency by finding the need-to-focus areas with just one prompt!
When Connectors Use the Wrong Sources
The launch brief you just got back looked clean and confident. But connectors can return outputs that look just as confident, even when built on the wrong inputs.
Connectors fail in four predictable ways:

• Stale data: The retrieval missed recent updates, and Claude doesn't flag it.
  • Permission gaps: Claude was blocked from a folder or thread it needed access to, and the output reflects only what it could see.
  • Too much context: Claude retrieved everything technically relevant, and the actual signal got buried.
  • File structure misreads: Claude pulled from the wrong tab, the template instead of the live doc, or an outdated version.
You only catch them by checking the inputs against what Claude reported.

Imagine you ask Claude to pull the pricing for an upcoming client proposal from your Drive's pricing folder.

Claude returns a clean breakdown. You drop them into the proposal and send it.

A day later, your sales lead flags that the numbers are 6 months out of date. The current pricing lives in a different file in the same folder.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! When a folder contains multiple files that match the prompt, Claude has to pick one, and without explicit instruction, it might pick a reasonable-looking, but wrong one. The fix is naming the exact source.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. Time scope isn't the issue, as both files exist right now. The Drive connector reads pricing fine; it's not a tool limitation. And Claude wasn't asked to compare versions, so reasoning didn't fail. Claude chose the wrong file from a folder of similar-looking options before reasoning ever started. The fix is naming the exact source.

options.label: The retrieval was scoped to a time window that excluded the current file
The Drive connector doesn't reliably read pricing data
Claude's reasoning failed to compare the two versions
Claude picked one of several matching files without knowing which was current

blocks.question: What is the most likely reason Claude pulled from the archived file instead of the current one?

blocks.text:
Each input failure mode has a specific fix:
  • Stale data → tighten the time scope or name the exact filter
  • Permission gaps → check what Claude actually has access to before re-prompting
  • Too much context → narrow the source to a specific folder, label, or project
  • File structure misreads → name the exact tab, version, or sub-document
If the inputs were right and the output is still off, then it's a reasoning problem.
blocks.title: 💡 Fixing the Input Issues

feedbackCorrect.text: Right on! Scanning multiple threads across a time window is exactly what a Gmail connector handles well — and exactly the kind of task that manual copy-paste makes tedious and error-prone. The connector retrieves; you review what Claude surfaces from it.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Assembling multiple email threads by hand introduces the risk of missing something and takes time that a connector removes. When the work involves pulling across several threads over a time window rather than analyzing one specific document, the connector is the cleaner path.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! For deep analysis of a single document, direct upload gives Claude complete, clean access to the full file. Email connectors read thread content and metadata reliably — but for a large document where every clause matters, manual upload is the more precise path.

When the task is analyzing a specific file rather than scanning across threads, connector retrieval adds a step without improving the result.

blocks.text: The Pattern Behind Any Connector Workflow
The scenario in this lesson used launch readiness, but the same structure can apply to various workflows:

• A client review
  • A hiring decision
  • A quarterly planning session
  • Or any situation where context is scattered across tools and needs to be synthesized into something actionable
Connect what the task requires, pair retrieval with a reasoning instruction, and let the output drive what happens next.

• Connectors pull live data from your tools. No more manual context gathering.
  • Good connector prompts have two layers: what to pull and what to do with it.
  • Multi-connector prompts enable cross-source insights. They help Claude synthesize related context from multiple sources.
  • Connectors aren't always best. Use uploads for focused, single-document analysis.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

You can now pull live context from across your tools in a single prompt, write retrieval and reasoning prompts, spot the ways connectors quietly fail, and tell when a connector beats a manual upload. In the next lesson, you'll push Claude's reasoning further with Thinking and Research — the modes that turn quick answers into deep, structured analysis. Together with Connectors, they make Claude useful for the work you've been putting off because it was too big to tackle on your own. Let's keep going!
The Right Tool at the Right Step

You can ask Claude anything and get a decent answer. But when the stakes are higher, decent isn't enough — how you set it up starts to matter. To solve this, Claude has distinct modes, and choosing the right one changes what you get. Imagine you're tackling a complex task and have quite a few very different problems to solve. Let's find out where each mode can be helpful and how!
Three Modes, One Project
Claude has three distinct modes — and using one at the wrong step is just as costly as not using it at all. Research, Thinking, and Web Search each do something the others can't.
Your Working Scenario

Imagine you run a growing business, and you're seriously considering expanding into a new product vertical — one you know something about, but haven't operated in. 

Before you commit budget, time, or team members, you want to know:

• Is this market actually worth entering right now?
  • Is the distribution channel you're counting on as strong as they claim?
Three Jobs, Three Modes

• You need to understand a space you've never operated in. That's Research: an autonomous multi-source investigation that returns a structured report.
  • You have the information, but the decision has real trade-offs. That's Thinking: Claude reasons step by step before responding, showing you the work, not just the conclusion.
  • One specific claim needs to be checked before you act on it. That's Web Search: live information pulled into your conversation.

Deciding whether a specific opportunity makes sense given several competing factors
Checking whether one specific claim holds up in independent sources

blocks.question: Before we go further, what do you think makes a task a good fit for Research over a standard Claude response?

blocks.text: Step 1: Get the Lay of the Land

Research is where you start when you need to understand a space you're not already inside. You're basically giving Claude a research brief. That means telling it which market to look at, which specific questions matter, how far back to go, and what to leave out.
How to Start a Research Session

In Claude, click the "Research" button before you submit your prompt. This tells Claude to run a full autonomous investigation rather than respond from its training. Research works better with Web Search enabled. This way, Claude can investigate across the web and internal sources.
A Brief vs. a Query

A query is a short instruction that tells Claude which topic to look into. A brief is a structured set of directions that tells Claude what questions to answer, how far back to look, and what to exclude. Research responds to whichever you give it — but the output quality reflects exactly that.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! There are no questions, no time window, and no exclusions here, so this is still a query. It tells Claude the topic, but not what to do with it. Research will return something, but not necessarily something you can act on.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. A brief sets the scope before the research starts: specific questions, a time horizon, and what to leave out. This example has none of those. It is a starting point, not a direction.

blocks.instruction: Identify if this is a brief or a query.

options.label: Query
Brief

blocks.question: "Research the productivity software market"

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! There are concrete questions and a clear constraint, so this is a brief. Research now has enough direction to return a report organized around the decision you need to make.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. This goes well beyond a topic label. It defines what to answer and adds a constraint. That structure is what turns a research session into a usable output.

options.label: Brief
Query

blocks.question: "Research the productivity software market — focus on tools for teams under 50 people and gaps in current reviews"

blocks.text: A Report Needs an Audit

Research pulls from open sources. The output looks clean and authoritative, but not every claim inside it can carry the same weight.

Before you build a decision on a Research report, you read it the way an editor reads a draft: looking for what's solid, what's thin, and what's missing.

• Unsupported claims: confident statements with no citation, or a citation that doesn't actually back the claim
  • Source gaps: questions in your brief that didn't get answered, or answered only from one type of source
  • Stale evidence: citations from years ago when your brief asked about the current state
blocks.title: 💡 Three Things to Check in Any Research Output

blocks.text: Read This Excerpt

Here's a section from a Research report on the productivity software market for small teams. Read it carefully — you'll spot the issues after. "Demand for productivity tools targeting small teams has grown significantly. Most competitors offer feature-heavy products, while async-first workflows remain underserved [Source: TechReview, 2021]. Pricing typically ranges from $8 to $15 per user per month, based on review aggregator data."

feedbackCorrect.text: All three are real flags. A confident claim without a citation is just an assertion. A 2021 source can't tell you what the market looks like now. And aggregator data shows what reviewers say, not what companies actually charge. Each one needs its own follow-up.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Specificity isn't a flaw — a precise claim is easier to verify than a vague one. The async-first claim could be checked with a targeted follow-up. The real issues are missing citations, stale dates, and narrow source types.

options.label: "Demand has grown significantly" — confident claim with no citation
Pricing data is sourced only from review aggregators — narrow source type
The citation is from 2021 — likely stale for a current decision
The claim about async-first workflows is too specific to verify

blocks.question: Which issues should you flag in that excerpt before acting on it?

blocks.exampleResponse: Follow-up findings: Current Q3 market data from Gartner confirms 14% year-over-year growth in the small-teams segment — the original "grown significantly" claim holds up but is now sourced. Demand evidence refreshed with two 2025 analyst reports (Forrester, IDC). Pricing range confirmed at $9-$16 via direct competitor pricing pages, slightly higher than aggregator data suggested.
blocks.prompt: Build the follow-up prompt that addresses the three issues you just identified.
blocks.template: Run a focused follow-up on the productivity tools report. Find a current source for [claim category] from the last [time frame]. Refresh the small-teams demand evidence with data from [source type]. And verify the pricing range from competitor pricing pages, not just review aggregators.

blocks.text: Now You Can Trust What's Left

Great job! After the audit and follow-up, the report has citations where it needed them, current data where it was stale, and a second source where it was narrow. That's a report you can build a decision on.
Step 2: Think It Through

You have the landscape. Now comes the harder question: Does moving into this market make sense for your business, right now, with the resources you have? This is where Thinking earns its place — applying rigorous analysis to a problem with real trade-offs, where the obvious answer isn't necessarily the right one.
When Thinking Is Worth It

Thinking mode adds genuine value when a problem has several competing factors — where variables interact, trade-offs don't have obvious winners, and the quality of the reasoning matters as much as the conclusion. 

But for a simple factual question, it adds waiting time without improving the answer.
How to Turn It On

To use Thinking, first make sure you’ve selected a current Claude model. Then, click Model Selector and toggle Thinking on. Good news: toggling it on doesn't start a new conversation — your existing chat stays intact, so you can switch it on at any point without losing your context.

When you turn on Thinking, Claude works through the problem step by step before producing a response — considering competing factors, testing different angles, and checking its own reasoning along the way. You see a summary of that process above the final answer, in an expandable "Thinking" section. Open it and read it. Reasoning is a valuable part of leading to a certain output.

Alongside Research principles, a few tweaks help Thinking reason better.
  • Give it the evidence to work with: The context or the key findings from your Research report, rather than asking it to reason from a general topic description.
  • Name the framework explicitly: "Apply Porter's Five Forces" gives the reasoning a structure.
  • Ask it to surface its assumptions: "List the assumptions this recommendation depends on" turns the output into something you can stress-test.
blocks.title: 💡 How to Get More From Thinking

correctTokens: the productivity tools for small teams
blocks.exampleResponse: Market Expansion Assessment Competitive intensity is moderate; established players are feature-heavy but slow to adapt. The async-first gap is real but narrow — two funded startups are targeting it. Key risks: long sales cycles, high content marketing cost to enter, and undifferentiated pricing. Recommendation: viable with a niche-first entry strategy and a 9-month runway commitment.
blocks.prompt: Complete the "Thinking" prompt using the research you just gathered.
blocks.template: Using the Research findings on [market segment], apply [analytical framework] to assess whether expanding into this vertical makes sense for a small business in year 3 of operation. Identify [number] biggest risks and evaluate whether the market gap in [specific opportunity] is real and accessible. End with a clear recommendation.
tokens: the productivity tools for small teams

blocks.text: Reading the Output as a Decision-Maker
The recommendation is only as reliable as the reasoning behind it. When you review the "Thinking" output, ask:

• Did it actually engage with the trade-offs?
  • Did it use the research findings, or did it reason from general knowledge?
If the reasoning feels thin or generic, the brief probably didn't give Claude enough to work with.
Same Prompt, Two Different Outputs

You ran the same market expansion question twice — once in standard mode, once with Thinking on. Both arrive at the same recommendation: enter the market.

Let's see where the Thinking shines.

Output 1: Standard mode output "Recommendation: Enter the market. The market is growing fast — 14% per year. Your product solves a real problem. It's simpler, focused on small teams, and priced for them from the start. That's a gap competitors haven't filled. The numbers support it too. Reaching customers in this space costs less than reaching enterprise customers, and small teams make decisions faster."

Output 2: Thinking mode output "Recommendation: Enter the market, but the brief got the reason wrong. The brief says to enter because the market is growing fast. Before I agree, I want to check that claim. The 14% growth is real for the whole market — but most of that growth comes from larger companies, not the small teams you'd be selling to. In the small-team segment specifically, growth is much slower (around 6-8%). So the answer is "enter", but not because the market is booming. The real opportunity is that existing tools don't fit small teams well."

feedbackCorrect.text: The two outputs use the same data, reach the same recommendation, and list the same next steps. The one thing Thinking did differently was interrogate the brief's premise — it questioned whether "growing demand" applied to small teams specifically, or only to the broader market.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Both outputs use the same source data, arrive at the same recommendation, and produce roughly the same set of next steps. None of those is where Thinking shows up. What changed in the Thinking output is that the underlying claim — "demand is growing" — got tested before being accepted.

options.label: It used more current market data
It listed more recommendations or next steps to take
It changed the recommendation itself
It questioned whether the "growing demand" claim applied to your case

blocks.question: Looking at both outputs, what did Thinking surface that the standard response didn't?

blocks.text: Step 3: Verify

Now, imagine this: the "Thinking" analysis flagged something worth checking before you commit. For example, you're counting on a specific distribution partner — a company called Prolvex — to reach your target market. They claim a strong reach with the customer segment you're targeting. Before you build your plan around that claim, you need to know if it holds up. Web Search can help you with exactly this.
Web Search Is for Specific Verification

Web Search is a precision tool. You can use it mid-conversation to check a specific claim, confirm a recent development, or pull one current data point — without leaving your analytical context or starting over.
One Setting to Check First

Before using Research, make sure Web Search is enabled. Before using Thinking, decide whether the reasoning also needs current web evidence. Thinking on Claude models uses it to pull live information mid-reasoning — without breaking out of the thought process to start a new conversation.

Web Search works best when the query mirrors how you'd brief a fact-checker — specific, bounded, and tied to one thing you need confirmed or ruled out:
  • Name the source type: "Analyst reports or customer reviews" cuts through irrelevant results better than an open query.
  • Set a time window: "In the last 12 months" prevents outdated results.
  • Frame it as a confirm-or-challenge: "Find coverage that confirms or challenges this claim" returns a more balanced result.
blocks.title: 💡 How to Get More From Web Search

blocks.text: The Sequence Is Not a Rule

Research → Thinking → Web Search is the natural order for a decision that starts with an unknown market. But the sequence shifts based on what you already know. The principle is that each mode serves a specific role, and you sequence them based on what your current step needs.

• Research starts with a brief: scope, questions, time horizon, and exclusions upfront, to produce a report built around your decision.
  • Thinking shows you the reasoning. Open the Thinking section and evaluate it, not just the recommendation beneath it.
  • Web Search is for precision. One specific claim, mid-conversation, without losing your analytical thread.
  • The sequence is a starting point. Rearrange it based on what each step actually needs.
  • Each mode has a job. Using the wrong mode for a task doesn't just underperform; it produces the wrong kind of output entirely.

blocks.text: What's Next

In the next lesson, you'll take the analysis you've built here and turn it into actual deliverables — a Word report, an Excel tracker, a PowerPoint deck — without opening another tool. 

Let's keep going!
Package Your Work

Suppose you've already done the analysis for your task. Now, it has to become a Word report for one person, an Excel tracker for another, and a deck for someone 10 minutes before a board meeting.

How do you reshape the same work without starting over each time? This lesson reduces all three to a single Claude conversation.
Scenario: Same Analysis, Three Audiences

Let's say you've just completed a market analysis for Mara Chen, a founder considering expanding her project management software into a new vertical. The analysis is done: you know which segment to target, why the timing is right, and what the risks are.
Now three people need that work in three different forms.

• Mara wants a written report she can share with her advisory board.
  • Her operations lead, David, needs a data table he can update with real numbers each month.
  • The board chair, who won't read a six-page report, needs a few slides before Thursday's meeting.
Why This Is the Hardest Part

The analysis took several hours. Now, packaging it for three audiences might take even more time: reformatting in Word, rebuilding formulas in Excel, and laying out slides in PowerPoint. The risk is also in producing something that's slightly inconsistent across all three because you made different decisions in each tool. File Creation wins you time in this case!
File Creation turns Claude's output into downloadable files — Word documents, Excel spreadsheets, PowerPoint decks, and PDFs — that you can share, edit, and present without switching to another tool.
What Happens When Claude Creates a File

When you ask Claude to create a file, it writes and runs code behind the scenes in a secure, private workspace, not just filling in a template.

That's why the Excel files have real formulas that work, Word docs have proper headings, and PowerPoint slides have proper layouts rather than plain text on a blank slide.

feedbackCorrect.text: The files Claude creates are structurally real — formulas calculate, heading styles apply, layouts hold. And the edit workflow is particularly powerful: upload a file, describe the change, and get an updated version. You never have to rebuild from scratch.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Claude doesn't self-verify files before delivery — reviewing the output is still your responsibility. The real advantages are structural: working formulas, proper formatting, and the ability to make targeted edits to existing files rather than starting over.

You can upload an existing file and ask Claude to make targeted edits to specific sections in the document
Claude produces Word documents with inherited heading styles and formatting

blocks.text: Enabling File Creation

To turn on File Creation, go to Settings → Capabilities and toggle on Code execution and file creation. Once enabled, Claude can produce downloadable files from any conversation. You'll see a download link appear directly below the file it creates. Files can also be saved straight to Google Drive if you prefer not to download them locally.
The Network Egress Setting
Directly below the File Creation toggle, you'll see Allow network egress — a setting that controls whether Claude can access the internet while building your files.

• "Off" keeps Claude entirely offline in its private workspace; documents still build, but no live data.
  • "On" enables internet access for research-backed files. For most document-creation work, leave it off. Turn it on when a task genuinely needs live data, and monitor the conversation while it runs.
Building the Written Report — Word

For a client-facing report, the brief matters more than the prompt. "Write a market analysis report" produces a generic document. A brief that specifies the structure, sections, the types of evidence each section should draw on, and the decision the report needs to support produces a review-ready document.

blocks.template:
Create a Word document: market expansion analysis for [audience].
Sections:
— Executive Summary (one page, leads with recommendation)
— Market Landscape (current players, gaps, recent changes)
— Opportunity Assessment ([framework])
— Risk Register (top [number] risks, each with likelihood and impact rating)
— Recommendation
Write in [voice direction]. Use formal heading styles. Base everything on these findings: *pasted findings*.

blocks.text: What Makes a Deliverable Shine
A file is review-ready when it can leave your hands without you flagging anything for the recipient. Four things separate a deliverable from a draft:

• Structural integrity: Formulas calculate, headings hold, layouts don't break.
  • Audience fit: The register, depth, and length match who's reading it.
  • Content completeness: Every section the brief specified is present and substantive.
  • Voice consistency: Sounds like the person sending it, not like a generic AI output.
If any of these is off, it's still a draft.

File Creation works best as an iterative loop rather than a single prompt.

Create the file, download it, review it, upload it back with specific edit instructions, and download the updated version. Each pass targets one problem — a section that's too long, a table that needs a new column, a slide that's missing speaker notes.
blocks.title: 💡 The "Upload → Edit → Download" Workflow

blocks.text: Read Before You Send

Download the report and read it the way the advisory board will. The structure looks right, the sections are all there — but read closely against the four criteria from earlier, and you'll find things that need a second pass.

feedbackCorrect.text: Three real problems. Voice mismatch will land wrong with a board that knows Mara's writing. Duplicated risks suggest sloppy analysis. A missing estimate in a section that promises one is incomplete. Page count by itself isn't a quality issue — the right length is the length the content needs.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Page count isn't a quality criterion unless the brief specified one. Six pages of substantive analysis are better than five padded ones. The other three options all fail one of the four criteria: voice fit, content quality, and completeness.

The Opportunity Assessment section references TAM but never provides the actual estimate
The Risk Register lists three risks, but two of them duplicate the same underlying concern

blocks.text: What's Next

In the next lesson, you'll learn how to organize your work and give Claude a persistent memory — setting up Projects so your context, constraints, and decisions carry across every conversation without you repeating them from scratch. Let's keep going!
Make Claude Work Your Way

You've shaped what Claude produces, such as documents that match your structure. But there's another layer: the process behind the work. The way you think about a problem. The framework you apply every time. This lesson is about packaging that into a Skill — so the next time you need it, Claude already knows how to run it.
From Format to Process

In the last lesson, you used pre-built Skills to produce Word, Excel, and PowerPoint files. Those handle format — they know how to build the artifact. Custom Skills handle process — the multi-step thinking you bring to recurring work.
There's a category of work you do the same way every time — and every time you do it, you explain it to Claude from scratch:

• How you structure a client check-in
  • How you evaluate a candidate after an interview
  • How you decide what to ship next
The process is consistent, and re-explaining is overwhelming.

feedbackCorrect.text: Skills earn their keep on work that repeats and carries judgment — the framework you apply, the steps in your preferred order, the standards you check against. One-off tasks don't benefit; the setup outlives the work.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A one-off task isn't worth the setup cost — by the time the Skill is built and tested, the work is done. Skills justify the investment when the work recurs, and the process is consistent.

options.label: A recurring deliverable type where the structure matters more than the content
A one-off task that requires careful thinking but won't repeat
A multi-step process you run roughly the same way every time, with your own judgment baked in
A framework you've developed that others on your team don't apply consistently

blocks.question: Which of these work patterns are good candidates for a custom Skill?

blocks.text: Scenario: Product Launch Retrospective
Remember a product launch you shipped in one of the earlier lessons? Let's say it went well, shipped on time, and the deliverables went out. Now what?
Your team is doing a retro. And if it goes the way some of these meetings go, it'll produce a list of more or less generic observations:

• Good comms
  • Tight timeline
  • Ship demos earlier next time
Nothing that actually changes how you launch next quarter. A custom Skill changes that.
Why Most Retros Are Weak

Most launch retros stay surface-level. What went well, what didn't, what to improve. The structure looks fine, but the thinking underneath it isn't doing real work. The retro that actually changes how you launch next time looks at the work differently.
Four Moves That Change the Retro
A stronger retro framework asks four things:

• Decisions vs. outcomes: Was the call right, even if the outcome was bad? Did you get lucky on a weak call?
  • Counterfactuals: What would a different choice have produced?
  • Luck identification: What worked for reasons you can't replicate?
  • Forward-looking lessons: What specifically changes for the next launch?
This is the thinking you can implement with Claude Skill.
What Is a Skill

Underneath, every Skill does two jobs: it recognizes when a request is the kind of work it's built for, and it carries out the steps for handling that work. The first job lives in a short description. The second lives in the instructions Claude follows once the Skill kicks in. Get the description right, and the Skill shows up at the right moment. Get the instructions right, and it does the right thing once it's there.
The Description Is the Trigger

Claude reads every conversation against your Skills' descriptions. When a request closely matches one, that Skill fires automatically, pulling in the instructions you wrote and applying them.

A description shouldn't be vague, as it might fire on the wrong work.
Where Skills Live in Claude

Custom Skills live under Customize → Skills, where you can see everything currently installed, toggle individual skills on or off, and add new ones. Two options appear here: Browse and Add. Browse skills opens the directory of pre-built Skills from Anthropic and partners, ready to install with a single click. Creating skills is where you build your own.
Worth a Look: Browse Skills

Before building your own, it's worth checking what already exists in the directory. Anthropic and its partners maintain a growing library, and some of the skills are useful for different kinds of work out of the box.

• /internal-comms packages company communication formats for routine internal writing.
  • /brand-guidelines applies a consistent visual identity across artifacts.
  • /learn is built for moments when you want to actually understand a topic rather than just get an answer, walking you through the why behind it.
  • /skill-creator, from Anthropic itself, helps you build new skills by interviewing you about your workflow.
Three Ways to Build Your Own
When you click "Create skill," Claude gives you three paths, each suited to a different starting point:

• Create with Claude opens a conversation in which Claude asks about the workflow, trigger phrasing, the inputs you'll provide, and the output you want.
  • Write skill instructions opens the manual editor, where you fill in the name, description, and instructions directly.
  • Upload a skill lets you bring in an already-built Skill (yours, a teammate's, etc.) as a ZIP file. Useful for sharing across a team or moving Skills between accounts.
Which Path Fits the Retro Skill

For the launch retro Skill, Create with Claude is the natural starting point. You have the framework in your head — the four moves — but writing the full Skill from scratch means thinking through trigger phrasing, edge cases, and instruction structure all at once. Letting Claude interview you surfaces those decisions one at a time. Let's walk through what that conversation looks like.
What Claude Asks
When you choose Create with Claude, it opens a chat focused entirely on building the Skill. The conversation covers:

• What the Skill does: the work it handles, in your own words. This becomes the instructions.
  • When it should fire: the phrasings you'd use to start this work. This becomes the description.
  • What inputs it expects: what you'll provide each time you trigger it.
  • What it produces: the structure and depth of the output.
  • A reference material: the output samples or supporting documents.
Claude asks one area or some of them at a time, then drafts the full Skill from your answers. You see the draft before saving.
Answering "What the Skill Does"

Your answer here becomes the instructions Claude follows when the Skill fires. This is where the four-moves framework becomes the Skill's actual content. blocks.title: Two Layers, Two Jobs

blocks.text:
• Custom Skills encode the thinking you bring to recurring work: Not templates, but multi-step processes with judgment built in.
  • The Skill's content is your framework. Generic instructions produce generic output, so the more specifically you describe the thinking, the more value the Skill carries.

  • The description is the trigger. Name the specific work it handles, the phrasings that should fire it, and what it explicitly does not handle.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

You have process, format, and voice all loaded into new conversations. The one thing still missing is context that follows you across projects entirely — who you are, what you do, the standards you hold in every conversation. That's Memory, and it's the last layer of the production stack.
The Layer That Knows You

You've spent the last few lessons building a working environment around Claude — context held in Projects, recurring processes held in Skills.

Each of those layers makes a single conversation start better than the last. There's one more layer. The one that means Claude opens every conversation already knowing how you work and what you care about. By the end of this lesson, you'll have that layer set up — and the habit of keeping it useful over time.

Let's get started!
Scenario: Months of Conversations
Imagine this: you moved into a new role a few months ago. Before, you were an individual contributor — running the analysis yourself, owning the deliverables. Now you lead a team of five.
Your work is different:

• More reviewing
  • More one-on-one meetings
  • More deciding what your team should focus on
You've used Claude through all of it. The old role, the transition, the new one. And Claude's been building a summary of useful work context from your conversations.
The Feature Behind the Scenes
That profile is Memory — Claude's ability to carry context about you across conversations. Memory is different from Projects:

• Projects hold context for a specific body of work: the documents, the team list, the decisions, and the deliverables tied to that particular effort.
  • Memory holds context about you: your role, your tools, your standards, your writing preferences, and the things you've told Claude over the months you've used it.
Depending on your plan and settings, Memory or chat search may already be enabled. Today, you’ll check what Claude can remember or reference.
The Same Question, Twice
Before opening Memory, let's see why it matters. The same prompt, run two ways — once in a fresh account with no profile, once in your account with Memory configured.

— Any specific topics you want to cover or any tensions in the relationship I should know about? 

Once I have that context, I can suggest some structure and questions worth asking.

blocks.text: What Memory Stores
Memory captures the kinds of things you'd tell a new colleague over the first few weeks of working together:

• Your role
  • The tools you use
  • Who's on your team
  • How you like things written
  • Recurring projects
  • Working preferences
Claude's Memory is designed to focus on useful work-related context. Still, avoid putting passwords, sensitive personal data, or confidential information into Memory.
Two Toggles, One Setting
Memory lives under Settings → Capabilities. You'll find two related toggles there:

• "Generate memory from chat history" controls whether Claude builds and updates your profile from conversations.
  • "Search and reference chats" controls whether Claude can reference specific past conversations when relevant.
Both can be on, both can be off, or you can use one without the other.
Time to Look

When both toggles are on, you'll see View and edit memory. Click it, and the Manage memory panel opens — a full list of everything Claude currently remembers about you. Your accumulated profile looks like a mix of stable facts about your work, things you told Claude explicitly, and things Claude inferred from patterns in your conversations.
Read through it slowly the first time. Three categories will start to show up:

• Accurate: things that are true and worth keeping
  • Outdated: things that used to be true and aren't anymore
  • Inferred wrongly: things Claude concluded from patterns that don't actually hold
The third category is the tricky one. These entries look like facts, but they were never stated explicitly. Claude made a reasonable guess based on your conversations, but it was off.

blocks.question: Looking at your accumulated profile, which entries should you flag for editing?

blocks.text: Why Inferred Entries Are the Risky Ones

Outdated entries are easy to spot once you look: a project name, an old title, a task you used to own. You read them and immediately know what's stale.

Inferred entries are harder. Claude didn't make them up — it concluded them from real patterns in your conversations. The depth preference came from months of you asking for a detailed analysis. The conclusions were reasonable, but they no longer hold.
How to Fix Each Kind

Outdated entries get deleted or replaced. Click the entry in the Manage memory panel and remove it, or edit it to reflect what's true now. Inferred entries need correction. You need to explicitly give Claude the correct version.
Two Ways to Update Memory
Once you've identified what needs to change, there are two ways to make the edit:

• In conversation, tell Claude directly what you want it to remember, in any chat.
  • In the Manage memory panel, find the specific entry, click the "Edit" button, and tell Claude what to edit or delete.
Which way fits depends on what you're changing.
When Each Method Fits

The Manage memory panel is the right tool when you want to see what Claude knows about you and shape it deliberately. You open it to scan the full profile and fix anything that's off. In-conversation editing is the right tool for in-the-moment additions. Something comes up you want Claude to remember going forward — a new preference, a context shift, a fact you forgot to mention — and you tell it directly in chat. No need to leave the conversation to update a panel.

blocks.text: Memory From Another AI

If you've been using ChatGPT or another assistant, you have months of accumulated context sitting in their memory. Claude has an import tool that pulls that context over.

You'll find it in the same Memory settings panel. The process is straightforward: you click "Start Import," copy a prompt in the other AI, paste the result into Claude's memory settings, and Claude integrates it.
Imported memory needs the same audit treatment. Other AIs make their own inferences from their own patterns, and those don't always travel cleanly.

blocks.text: What Belongs Where
Now that you've seen Memory in action, the question gets sharper: what should live there?

• Memory is for you — the things that stay true across all your work.
  • Projects are for work — the things specific to one body of effort.
  • Skills are for process — recurring work with judgment baked in.
The most common Memory mistake is putting project-specific context into Memory, where it pollutes every unrelated conversation.

In practice, all these layers blend. A single Claude response can carry contributions from all four — and learning to recognize which layer is doing what is the synthesis skill that makes the whole stack feel coherent.
