• Projects hold context for a specific body of work: the documents, the team list, the decisions, and the deliverables tied to that particular effort.
  • Memory holds context about you: your role, your tools, your standards, your writing preferences, and the things you've told Claude over the months you've used it.
Depending on your plan and settings, Memory or chat search may already be enabled. Today, you’ll check what Claude can remember or reference.
The Same Question, Twice
Before opening Memory, let's see why it matters. The same prompt, run two ways — once in a fresh account with no profile, once in your account with Memory configured.

blocks.exampleResponse:
I'd be glad to help you prep. To give you useful talking points, I'll need a few things first: 

— Who is John — a direct report, a peer, your manager? 
— What's the agenda for the meeting, or is it an open one-on-one? 
— Any specific topics you want to cover or any tensions in the relationship I should know about? 

Once I have that context, I can suggest some structure and questions worth asking.
blocks.prompt: This is what the prompt looks like in a fresh Claude account. Fill in the gaps to see how it responds when it doesn't know you yet.
blocks.template: Help me prep talking points for [meeting type] tomorrow with [name]

blocks.text:
A reasonable response, but one that puts the work back on you. You have to type out everything Claude needs before you can get to the actual prep.

Now let's try the same prompt — but in your account, where Claude has been building a profile of you for months.

blocks.exampleResponse:
For your one-on-one with John, here are talking points organized by what usually matters most in your one-on-ones with direct reports: 

— Where is he on the redesign project (you flagged last week that the timeline felt tight)?
— How is he feeling about the workload after Kenji's departure?
— One open-ended check-in question on his career goals — you mentioned wanting to be more deliberate about those conversations.

Want me to draft the opening question for each?
blocks.prompt: Fill in the gaps in the same prompt, now in your account, to see what changes when Claude already knows you.
blocks.template: Help me prep talking points for [meeting type] tomorrow with [name]

feedbackCorrect.text: That's the shift Memory makes. The first response treats you as a stranger and gathers context before being useful. The second one opens already knowing the relationship, the work in progress, and what you've been thinking about — because you've told Claude those things across previous conversations.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The prompt was identical in both cases. The difference is that Claude already had context from months of conversations with you. General management knowledge would have produced a generic answer, not one referencing John's specific project and a team member by name.

options.label: The second response draws on Claude's general knowledge about management practices
The second response uses better reasoning to anticipate what a one-on-one usually covers
The second response builds on the context Claude already had, instead of asking you to provide it
The second response is shaped by a more thoughtful prompt than the first

blocks.question: What's the most important difference between the two outputs?

blocks.text: What Memory Stores
Memory captures the kinds of things you'd tell a new colleague over the first few weeks of working together:

• Your role
  • The tools you use
  • Who's on your team
  • How you like things written
  • Recurring projects
  • Working preferences
Claude's Memory is designed to focus on useful work-related context. Still, avoid putting passwords, sensitive personal data, or confidential information into Memory.
Two Toggles, One Setting
Memory lives under Settings → Capabilities. You'll find two related toggles there:

• "Generate memory from chat history" controls whether Claude builds and updates your profile from conversations.
  • "Search and reference chats" controls whether Claude can reference specific past conversations when relevant.
Both can be on, both can be off, or you can use one without the other.
Time to Look

When both toggles are on, you'll see View and edit memory. Click it, and the Manage memory panel opens — a full list of everything Claude currently remembers about you. Your accumulated profile looks like a mix of stable facts about your work, things you told Claude explicitly, and things Claude inferred from patterns in your conversations.
Read through it slowly the first time. Three categories will start to show up:

• Accurate: things that are true and worth keeping
  • Outdated: things that used to be true and aren't anymore
  • Inferred wrongly: things Claude concluded from patterns that don't actually hold
The third category is the tricky one. These entries look like facts, but they were never stated explicitly. Claude made a reasonable guess based on your conversations, but it was off.

feedbackCorrect.text: Two entries to flag, each a different kind of problem. The quarterly analysis line is outdated, and the response-depth line is an inference Claude made from old conversations that doesn't fit the new role. Each one needs a different fix.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Leading a small team is accurate and current, so it stays. The other two all need attention — but for different reasons. Memory accumulates all kinds of entries, and the audit is what separates them.

options.label: "User prefers detailed, analytical responses" — Claude inferred this from past conversations; you now usually need executive-level summaries
"User leads a small team" — Claude inferred it from the past conversations after you shifted the role
"User is responsible for delivering the quarterly competitive analysis" — was true six months ago, before the role change

blocks.question: Looking at your accumulated profile, which entries should you flag for editing?

blocks.text: Why Inferred Entries Are the Risky Ones

Outdated entries are easy to spot once you look: a project name, an old title, a task you used to own. You read them and immediately know what's stale.

Inferred entries are harder. Claude didn't make them up — it concluded them from real patterns in your conversations. The depth preference came from months of you asking for a detailed analysis. The conclusions were reasonable, but they no longer hold.
How to Fix Each Kind

Outdated entries get deleted or replaced. Click the entry in the Manage memory panel and remove it, or edit it to reflect what's true now. Inferred entries need correction. You need to explicitly give Claude the correct version.
Two Ways to Update Memory
Once you've identified what needs to change, there are two ways to make the edit:

• In conversation, tell Claude directly what you want it to remember, in any chat.
  • In the Manage memory panel, find the specific entry, click the "Edit" button, and tell Claude what to edit or delete.
Which way fits depends on what you're changing.
When Each Method Fits

The Manage memory panel is the right tool when you want to see what Claude knows about you and shape it deliberately. You open it to scan the full profile and fix anything that's off. In-conversation editing is the right tool for in-the-moment additions. Something comes up you want Claude to remember going forward — a new preference, a context shift, a fact you forgot to mention — and you tell it directly in chat. No need to leave the conversation to update a panel.

blocks.prompt: You're correcting the inferred response-depth entry in the conversation. Write the instruction.
blocks.template: I now [role context]. I usually need [response depth] for day-to-day work, not deep analytical detail. Remember this. [Command] before producing a long-form response on something.

blocks.text: Memory From Another AI

If you've been using ChatGPT or another assistant, you have months of accumulated context sitting in their memory. Claude has an import tool that pulls that context over.

You'll find it in the same Memory settings panel. The process is straightforward: you click "Start Import," copy a prompt in the other AI, paste the result into Claude's memory settings, and Claude integrates it.
Imported memory needs the same audit treatment. Other AIs make their own inferences from their own patterns, and those don't always travel cleanly.
blocks.title: 💡 One Thing Worth Noting

blocks.text: What Belongs Where
Now that you've seen Memory in action, the question gets sharper: what should live there?

• Memory is for you — the things that stay true across all your work.
  • Projects are for work — the things specific to one body of effort.
  • Skills are for process — recurring work with judgment baked in.
The most common Memory mistake is putting project-specific context into Memory, where it pollutes every unrelated conversation.

feedbackCorrect.text: Exactly! This is true across every conversation you have, regardless of what you're working on. Memory holds it.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Not quite. This isn't tied to a specific project — it's true everywhere. Memory holds the things that stay true about you across all work; Projects hold the things specific to one effort.

blocks.instruction: Sort this piece of context by where it belongs.

options.label: Project
Memory

blocks.question: "I lead a team of five product specialists"

feedbackCorrect.text: This is specific to one body of work, time-limited, and will be irrelevant in 6 weeks. This belongs in a Project, where it can be part of that workstream's context without affecting unrelated conversations.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Project-specific deadlines pollute Memory. They become outdated quickly, they don't apply to other work, and they accumulate as stale entries. Keep them where the work lives — in the Project.

blocks.instruction: And where does this one belong?

options.label: Project
Memory

blocks.question: "The redesign project deadline is the third Friday of next month"

feedbackCorrect.text: This is a writing preference that applies everywhere — your work, personal projects, and communication style. Memory holds it, so Claude applies it consistently.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A writing preference isn't project-specific. It's something true about you across all contexts, which puts it firmly in Memory's territory.

options.label: Project
Memory

blocks.question: "I prefer responses without hedging language like 'might' or 'could potentially'"

blocks.text: The Production Stack, Working Together

In practice, all these layers blend. A single Claude response can carry contributions from all four — and learning to recognize which layer is doing what is the synthesis skill that makes the whole stack feel coherent.

feedbackCorrect.text: Memory carries who you are and how you write. The Project carries the specific launch context. The Skill carries the framework. The output reads like one thing, but it's four layers doing coordinated work.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Each layer is doing visible work in this output. Memory is in the role and voice baseline. The Project is in the launch-specific references. The Skill is in the structured framework. Removing any would change the output.

options.label: Project — Claude is pulling the specific launch documents and context
Memory — Claude knows your role and preferences
Skill — the four-moves framework is being run on the launch

blocks.question: You ask Claude in your launch retro Project, "Run the retro for the redesign launch." Claude produces a structured retro using the four-moves framework, in your direct plain-language voice, referencing the specific launch documents from the Project. Which layers are visibly contributing?

blocks.text: Memory and Your Personal Projects
One thing worth noting: most people use Claude for more than work. Personal writing, travel planning, helping a kid with homework, and the side project. Memory accumulates from all of it.

That's fine — but it means your professional profile gets mixed with hobby context and one-off mentions. Periodically, you'll want to clean Memory specifically for your professional work: remove personal entries that aren't useful, keep the ones that are, and make sure the work-relevant profile is clean.

The audit habit applies across both. Just be deliberate about which kind of entry you're keeping.
The Audit Habit

Memory rewards maintenance. The profile that worked 6 months ago doesn't necessarily work today, and the longer it goes unchecked, the more stale entries accumulate.

Two cadences are worth setting:

• Monthly check-in: Open "Manage memory," scan for outdated entries, and fix the inferences that don't hold anymore.
  • Trigger-based audit: Every time something material changes (new role, new project, new direction), audit Memory specifically against that change.

• Memory carries who you are across conversations. Role, tools, preferences, working style; the things that stay true regardless of what you're working on.
  • Memory is on by default. That means Claude has been remembering things about you, whether you've configured it or not.
  • Three categories of entry: accurate (keep), outdated (replace), inferred wrongly (correct explicitly).
  • Two methods for updating memory: The Manage memory panel for deliberate audits and structural fixes, in-conversation edits for in-the-moment additions you want Claude to remember going forward.
  • Each layer has a job: Memory for you, Projects for the work, and Skills for the process.
  • Audit monthly, and on every major change. Stale Memory is worse than no Memory.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next

You've built the production stack — Memory, Projects, Skills, plus the connector and reasoning layers from earlier in this course. Every new conversation now opens with Claude already loaded for your work. In the next lesson, you'll start using Claude to build with you. Advanced Artifacts — interactive tools that hold their own data across sessions, call Claude from inside themselves to handle the work, and can be shared with people who don't have Claude at all. Let's keep going!
Build Something With Claude

In the last lessons, you've been configuring Claude to work the way you do. Every conversation now opens with Claude already loaded for the work ahead. This lesson is different. Instead of configuring Claude to help you better, you'll build something with Claude — an Artifact — a working interactive tool that holds its own data and makes its own moves. Let's get started!
What's an Artifact?

You've likely seen Artifacts before — the side panel that appears when you ask Claude to build something interactive: a chart, a calculator, a small webpage, or a draft document you can edit in place.

Artifacts are how Claude builds things you can actually use, right inside the conversation. No deployment, hosting, or separate tool to open. The artifact appears in a panel beside the chat. You interact with it directly, and it updates as you ask for changes.
Display Artifacts vs. Functional Artifacts
There's a distinction worth being explicit about:

• A display Artifact shows you something — a generated chart, a formatted document, a diagram, a styled webpage. It's a visual output.
  • A functional Artifact does something — it takes input from you, processes it, and produces a result that depends on what you put in.
This lesson focuses on functional Artifacts because they behave more like small tools than static outputs.
Basic vs. Advanced Artifacts

A basic functional Artifact runs once — you open it, use it, close the conversation, and the data is gone. That's fine for a quick calculator or one-time tool.

A more advanced Artifact is different.
Three capabilities together separate it from the basic version:

• Persistent storage: The Artifact saves data between sessions, so it remembers what you did last time.
  • AI inside the Artifact: The Artifact can call Claude directly to handle context-sensitive work.
  • Publishing: The Artifact can be shared with people without a Claude account via a single link.
Together, these turn an Artifact from a throwaway demo into a tool you return to.

feedbackCorrect.text: Three capabilities do different jobs. Persistent storage handles state; AI inside handles judgment-adjacent work that the rules can't reach; publishing handles sharing. Generating the interface happens at build time when you're asking Claude to make the Artifact — that's a Claude capability, not an Artifact capability.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Interface generation happens at build time, when you describe the Artifact to Claude — that's Claude building the tool. The three correct options describe what the Artifact does while in use: storage holds the data, AI inside handles work the rules can't reach, publishing puts the tool in someone else's hands.

options.label: Persistent storage lets the Artifact hold data across sessions — a log, a tracker, anything that compounds in value over time
Publishing lets you share the Artifact with someone who doesn't have a Claude account, via a link
AI inside the Artifact lets it interpret user input that pure code can't — like reading the user's notes about how a workout felt
AI inside the Artifact lets it generate the entire interface from a single description

blocks.question: Let's test your understanding! Which statements correctly describe what each capability enables?

blocks.text: Scenario: Your Progress Tracker

Let's say you've decided to train for a half-marathon. Your target date is twelve weeks out. You currently run 5K comfortably twice a week. To get from where you are to a finished half-marathon, you need a real training plan and the discipline to follow it.
You want a tool that can:

• Log your sessions
  • Adapt your training plan based on what you did
  • Be shared with a friend who's training for the same race
An Artifact handles all three. It logs, adapts, and lives in a link you can open from anywhere.
Specification Comes Before Building
Every Artifact specification needs four things:

• Inputs = what the user provides and in what shape
  • Processing logic = what happens to the input
  • Output = what the user sees in return
  • Edge cases = the situations that aren't the happy path
Write these down before you write the prompt that builds the Artifact.

correctTokens: reset the progression to the last completed long run
blocks.exampleResponse: Specification saved. The Artifact will log sessions (date, type, duration, distance, perceived effort, notes), apply progression rules based on the last 2 weeks of data, use AI inside the Artifact to interpret subjective notes for fatigue or injury flags, and reset the long-run progression to the user's last completed distance if a skipped week is detected. Ready to start the build.
blocks.prompt: Complete the specification in the chat before building. Each gap defines one part of the Artifact.
blocks.template:
I want to build a tracker for a half-marathon training in 12 weeks. Before building, here is a specification. Analyze it.
Inputs: For each session — [session field]. Stored in persistent storage. *Pasted training data example*
Logic: Apply progression rules based on the last [time frame]. AI inside the Artifact reads subjective notes and flags patterns.
Output: Session log, next-session recommendation with reasoning, week-view, trend view.
Edge case + handler: [edge case] — [handler command].
tokens: reset the progression to the last completed long run

blocks.text: The Build Order
For a tool with persistent data, the iteration order goes in the following passes:

• Pass 1: Data structure. What gets stored, what shape, what fields
  • Pass 2: Logic. The rules that produce recommendations, plus the AI moments
  • Pass 3: Interface. How the user sees and edits the data
  • Edge cases handled throughout, not at the end
How the Build Conversation Works

Building an Artifact is a conversation. You hand Claude the spec, then walk through each pass with a focused prompt for that pass. Claude builds, you review what appeared in the side panel, confirm or adjust, and move to the next pass.

The mistake is asking Claude to build the whole thing from the spec in one prompt. The result is impressive in version one and impossible to iterate on. Building in passes keeps each layer focused and reviewable.
Pass 1: Data Structure and Storage

The first prompt establishes what the Artifact remembers. You describe the shape of each session entry and tell Claude to use persistent storage so the data carries across sessions after the Artifact is published and storage is available.

The data structure decides what the rest of the Artifact can do. Get this pass right, and the next two are much easier.

Let's try that in action.

blocks.prompt: Write the first build prompt in the same chat. Each gap defines part of what gets stored.
blocks.template: Build an Artifact for training tracking. Each session entry should store [session fields], perceived effort, and notes. Use [storage type] so data carries across sessions.

blocks.text: Verify Before Moving On

During development, test the UI and data flow. For persistent storage, publish the Artifact first (you'll see how to do it further in the lesson), then add test entries, reopen the published Artifact, and confirm the data persists. The Artifact's storage is limited to about 20 MB, which is plenty for a 12-week training block.
Pass 2: Logic
The second pass adds the recommendation logic. Two kinds of work happen here:

• Rule-based logic handles the math: progression rates, recovery patterns, goal-distance planning. This is regular JavaScript inside the Artifact.
  • AI inside the Artifact handles what the rules can't read — your notes about how a session felt.
You still decide. The AI is doing pattern recognition on what you wrote.

blocks.prompt: Write the prompt that adds the recommendation logic.
blocks.template:
Add recommendation logic to the Artifact.
Apply progression rules: [progression rule] by no more than 10% per week, suggest recovery after hard sessions, and work backward from the 12-week goal.
When I log notes about how a session felt, use [AI feature] to read the notes and surface flags, like a pattern of tightness across the week.

blocks.text: AI inside the Artifact handles work the rules can't reach. When you log "legs felt heavy", AI inside the Artifact reads the note and surfaces a flag — "You've mentioned tightness three times this week. Consider an easier session or a rest day before the next long run."
Pass 3: Interface
The interface is the thinnest layer but the one that gets the most attention from users. For the training tracker, four views matter:

• A session entry form: quick to fill, defaults sensible
  • The next session recommendation: what to do, when, and why (the reasoning matters as much as the recommendation)
  • The week-view of the upcoming plan: what the rest of the week looks like
  • The trend view: distance and frequency over time, ideally as a simple chart
Good Artifact interfaces don't require explanation. If the user has to ask what something means, the interface failed.

blocks.prompt: Write the prompt that brings the interface together.
blocks.template:
Refine the interface. Build four views:
  1. [View 1] with sensible defaults
  2. The next-session recommendation showing what to do, when, and [reasoning element]
  3. A week-view of the rest of the planned week
  4. A trend view showing [trend data] as a simple chart

blocks.text: Read It Like a Stranger

With the interface in place, the Artifact is now functional. The last review is the hardest one: walk through it as if you've never seen it before. Open the entry form. Are the fields self-explanatory? Read the next session recommendation. Does the reasoning make sense without your context? Check the week-view. Could you act on it cold? If anything makes you stop and think, "What does this mean?" — the interface failed there.
The Edge Cases
The Artifact has to handle situations that aren't in the textbook progression:

• A skipped week: the user didn't run at all for 7 days
  • A session that doesn't match the plan: they were supposed to do intervals, but did an easy run instead
  • Injury flags: multiple consecutive notes mentioning pain or tightness
  • Behind the goal-distance curve: 6 weeks out, the long run is still at 10K when it should be at 15K
  • Ahead of the goal-distance curve: the user is feeling strong and progressing faster than planned
Each one needs an explicit handler in the logic. Without that, the Artifact confidently gives wrong recommendations.
Iterating Without Breaking What Works

The temptation when fixing one issue is to ask Claude to rebuild the Artifact. That regresses the parts that were already working. The better move is targeted iteration. Describe the problem, not the fix. Name the specific behavior that's wrong, the specific scenario where it appears, and what the correct behavior should be.

correctTokens: a gap of more than 7 days between sessions
blocks.exampleResponse: Updated the skipped-week handler. The progression now resets to the user's last completed long run when more than 7 days have passed without a logged session, and rebuilds the plan from that point. The rest of the recommendation logic and the AI note-interpretation are unchanged. The trend view will now show the gap clearly.
blocks.prompt: One specific edge case isn't handled. Write the iteration prompt that fixes it without regressing the rest.
blocks.template: The Artifact currently produces [problem behavior] when the user logs [trigger scenario]. The correct behavior should be [intended behavior] to the last completed long run distance. Apply this fix to [specific component] without changing the rest of the Artifact's logic.
tokens: a gap of more than 7 days between sessions

blocks.text: Sharing the Artifact
Once the build holds up, sharing makes the Artifact accessible to your friend. In the top-right of the Artifact panel, click Publish artifact. A Share artifact dialog opens with two options:

• Publish to web — anyone with the link can view, and the Artifact may appear in search engine results. The chat stays private.
  • Share with your team — teammates with the link can view (Team plan only).
When Your Friend Opens the Link

You've built the tracker. You've iterated through three passes. You publish the Artifact and send the link to your friend, who's training for the same half-marathon.

They open the link cold with no context, conversation history, or an idea of how the inputs work.

This is the test. If they get confused, the Artifact isn't done.
A Different Build, Same Use Case

Imagine a colleague built their own training tracker for the same goal. Their version is functional, but it makes different choices from yours. They've sent it to you to look at. Read what they built — not the code, but the behavior. What does a non-builder actually encounter when they open it for the first time?
How to Read an Artifact Like a Non-Builder
When you audit a tool you didn't build, the trick is to forget your assumptions. Ask:

• Can a first-time user figure out what to do without instruction?
  • Are the input fields self-explanatory, or do they require knowledge the builder forgot to surface?
  • Does the output explain itself, or does it require the builder's mental model to make sense?
  • Are the edge cases handled, or do they produce wrong-but-confident output?
The answers distinguish a tool worth sending from one that needs more work.

feedbackCorrect.text: Three real issues. Unexplained jargon ("PE") confuses anyone who isn't the builder. Recommendations without reasoning leave users without the context they need to trust or override. An AI inside the Artifact that isn't actually reading the notes is a feature that exists in the spec but not in the build. The week-view starting day is a preference, not a quality issue.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Days of the week starting on Monday vs. Sunday is a regional preference, not a defect. Some users prefer one, some prefer the other. The other three options all break the "a non-builder could use this" standard — unexplained jargon, missing reasoning, and a broken AI feature would each immediately confuse a first-time user.

options.label: When the user logs an injury note in the free-text field, the Artifact gives the same recommendation as if nothing was logged — the AI inside the Artifact isn't reading the notes at all
The session entry form has a field labeled "PE" with no explanation — most users won't know it means perceived effort
The recommendation says "do an easy run tomorrow" without explaining why, leaving the user uncertain about whether the recommendation accounts for their recent training
The week-view shows the days of the week starting on Monday instead of Sunday

blocks.question: Reading your colleague's training tracker, which issues would a first-time user actually hit?

blocks.text: When an Artifact Is the Right Tool
The training tracker works as an Artifact because two things line up:

• The data fits comfortably in persistent storage.
  • The user wants to share it with people who don't have Claude.
When those things don't line up, another tool fits better:

• Claude Code for tools you'll run on your own machine that need full local access: reading and writing files on disk, running scripts, invoking other software, or operating on a schedule.
  • Cowork for work where Claude executes a multi-step task across your computer rather than building a tool you'll use again.
  • Claude Design for visual-first prototypes meant to be shown to stakeholders before any working tool is built — landing pages, mockups, decks.
You'll try all of them further in this course.

• Functional Artifacts are stateful, intelligent, and shareable. Persistent storage holds the data, AI inside handles work the rules can't reach, and publishing puts the tool in the hands of people who don't have Claude.
  • Write the specification before any prompt. Inputs, logic, output, and edge cases paired with their handlers; "what could go wrong" is part of the spec, not an afterthought.
  • Build in passes, not in one prompt. Data structure first, then logic, then interface, with edge cases handled throughout; each pass gets reviewed before the next one starts
  • Validate between passes. Log real sessions to confirm storage works, test recommendations after logic, walk the interface as a first-time user. Skipping validation is how bugs survive into the final version.
  • The real test is whether someone else can use it cold. Your understanding of how the tool works hides issues a non-builder hits immediately, which is what the audit step exists to surface.
  • Iterate by describing the problem, not the fix. Name the wrong behavior, the trigger scenario, and the intended behavior; let Claude apply the fix to the specific component without rebuilding the rest.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next

Great job! You've built a tool that holds its own state, makes its own moves, and can be opened by anyone with the link. That's a real shift in what you can do with Claude.

The next step pushes further in the same direction. Instead of building tools you and others use interactively, you'll start working with Claude as something that can take a brief and execute on its own — across your files, your apps, and your desktop. The agentic side of Claude begins next. Let's keep going!

• Log your sessions

How the Build Conversation Works

Building an Artifact is a conversation. You hand Claude the spec, then walk through each pass with a focused prompt for that pass. Claude builds, you review what appeared in the side panel, confirm or adjust, and move to the next pass.

The mistake is asking Claude to build the whole thing from the spec in one prompt. The result is impressive in version one and impossible to iterate on. Building in passes keeps each layer focused and reviewable.

Pass 2: Logic
The second pass adds the recommendation logic. Two kinds of work happen here:

• Rule-based logic handles the math: progression rates, recovery patterns, goal-distance planning. This is regular JavaScript inside the Artifact.
  • AI inside the Artifact handles what the rules can't read — your notes about how a session felt.
You still decide. The AI is doing pattern recognition on what you wrote.

content.value: AI inside the Artifact handles work the rules can't reach. When you log "legs felt heavy", AI inside the Artifact reads the note and surfaces a flag — "You've mentioned tightness three times this week. Consider an easier session or a rest day before the next long run."
Pass 3: Interface
The interface is the thinnest layer but the one that gets the most attention from users. For the training tracker, four views matter:

• A session entry form: quick to fill, defaults sensible
  • The next session recommendation: what to do, when, and why (the reasoning matters as much as the recommendation)
  • The week-view of the upcoming plan: what the rest of the week looks like
  • The trend view: distance and frequency over time, ideally as a simple chart
Good Artifact interfaces don't require explanation. If the user has to ask what something means, the interface failed.

content.value: Read It Like a Stranger

With the interface in place, the Artifact is now functional. The last review is the hardest one: walk through it as if you've never seen it before. Open the entry form. Are the fields self-explanatory? Read the next session recommendation. Does the reasoning make sense without your context? Check the week-view. Could you act on it cold? If anything makes you stop and think, "What does this mean?" — the interface failed there.
The Edge Cases
The Artifact has to handle situations that aren't in the textbook progression:

• A skipped week: the user didn't run at all for 7 days
  • A session that doesn't match the plan: they were supposed to do intervals, but did an easy run instead
  • Injury flags: multiple consecutive notes mentioning pain or tightness
  • Behind the goal-distance curve: 6 weeks out, the long run is still at 10K when it should be at 15K
  • Ahead of the goal-distance curve: the user is feeling strong and progressing faster than planned
Each one needs an explicit handler in the logic. Without that, the Artifact confidently gives wrong recommendations.
Iterating Without Breaking What Works

The temptation when fixing one issue is to ask Claude to rebuild the Artifact. That regresses the parts that were already working. The better move is targeted iteration. Describe the problem, not the fix. Name the specific behavior that's wrong, the specific scenario where it appears, and what the correct behavior should be.

When Your Friend Opens the Link

You've built the tracker. You've iterated through three passes. You publish the Artifact and send the link to your friend, who's training for the same half-marathon.

They open the link cold with no context, conversation history, or an idea of how the inputs work.

This is the test. If they get confused, the Artifact isn't done.
A Different Build, Same Use Case

Imagine a colleague built their own training tracker for the same goal. Their version is functional, but it makes different choices from yours. They've sent it to you to look at. Read what they built — not the code, but the behavior. What does a non-builder actually encounter when they open it for the first time?
https://d2h7i1o4snhir4.cloudfront.net/page-fragments/21720f3f-44c6-4bfe-a089-01dd9e2a94a8.webp
How to Read an Artifact Like a Non-Builder
When you audit a tool you didn't build, the trick is to forget your assumptions. Ask:

• Can a first-time user figure out what to do without instruction?
  • Are the input fields self-explanatory, or do they require knowledge the builder forgot to surface?
  • Does the output explain itself, or does it require the builder's mental model to make sense?
  • Are the edge cases handled, or do they produce wrong-but-confident output?
The answers distinguish a tool worth sending from one that needs more work.

feedback_correct.text: Three real issues. Unexplained jargon ("PE") confuses anyone who isn't the builder. Recommendations without reasoning leave users without the context they need to trust or override. An AI inside the Artifact that isn't actually reading the notes is a feature that exists in the spec but not in the build. The week-view starting day is a preference, not a quality issue.

feedback_incorrect.text: Days of the week starting on Monday vs. Sunday is a regional preference, not a defect. Some users prefer one, some prefer the other. The other three options all break the "a non-builder could use this" standard — unexplained jargon, missing reasoning, and a broken AI feature would each immediately confuse a first-time user.

content.value: When an Artifact Is the Right Tool
The training tracker works as an Artifact because two things line up:

• The data fits comfortably in persistent storage.
  • The user wants to share it with people who don't have Claude.
When those things don't line up, another tool fits better:

• Claude Code for tools you'll run on your own machine that need full local access: reading and writing files on disk, running scripts, invoking other software, or operating on a schedule.
  • Cowork for work where Claude executes a multi-step task across your computer rather than building a tool you'll use again.
  • Claude Design for visual-first prototypes meant to be shown to stakeholders before any working tool is built — landing pages, mockups, decks.
You'll try all of them further in this course.

blocks.text: Build Something With Claude

In the last lessons, you've been configuring Claude to work the way you do. Every conversation now opens with Claude already loaded for the work ahead. This lesson is different. Instead of configuring Claude to help you better, you'll build something with Claude — an Artifact — a working interactive tool that holds its own data and makes its own moves. Let's get started!
What's an Artifact?

You've likely seen Artifacts before — the side panel that appears when you ask Claude to build something interactive: a chart, a calculator, a small webpage, or a draft document you can edit in place.

Artifacts are how Claude builds things you can actually use, right inside the conversation. No deployment, hosting, or separate tool to open. The artifact appears in a panel beside the chat. You interact with it directly, and it updates as you ask for changes.
Display Artifacts vs. Functional Artifacts
There's a distinction worth being explicit about:

• A display Artifact shows you something — a generated chart, a formatted document, a diagram, a styled webpage. It's a visual output.
  • A functional Artifact does something — it takes input from you, processes it, and produces a result that depends on what you put in.
This lesson focuses on functional Artifacts because they behave more like small tools than static outputs.
Basic vs. Advanced Artifacts

A basic functional Artifact runs once — you open it, use it, close the conversation, and the data is gone. That's fine for a quick calculator or one-time tool.

A more advanced Artifact is different.
Three capabilities together separate it from the basic version:

• Persistent storage: The Artifact saves data between sessions, so it remembers what you did last time.
  • AI inside the Artifact: The Artifact can call Claude directly to handle context-sensitive work.
  • Publishing: The Artifact can be shared with people without a Claude account via a single link.
Together, these turn an Artifact from a throwaway demo into a tool you return to.

feedbackCorrect.text: Three capabilities do different jobs. Persistent storage handles state; AI inside handles judgment-adjacent work that the rules can't reach; publishing handles sharing. Generating the interface happens at build time when you're asking Claude to make the Artifact — that's a Claude capability, not an Artifact capability.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Interface generation happens at build time, when you describe the Artifact to Claude — that's Claude building the tool. The three correct options describe what the Artifact does while in use: storage holds the data, AI inside handles work the rules can't reach, publishing puts the tool in someone else's hands.

options.label: Persistent storage lets the Artifact hold data across sessions — a log, a tracker, anything that compounds in value over time
Publishing lets you share the Artifact with someone who doesn't have a Claude account, via a link
AI inside the Artifact lets it interpret user input that pure code can't — like reading the user's notes about how a workout felt
AI inside the Artifact lets it generate the entire interface from a single description

Build the Tool That Does Your Work

You've been configuring Claude, building Artifacts, and shaping how every conversation starts. Now you'll take a different step — building a real, working tool on your computer that handles a piece of your professional work end to end. A script you run when you need it, that takes inputs and produces a finished deliverable.

That's what Claude Code is for. By the end of this lesson, you'll have a working tool, and you'll know the limits of what's worth building this way. 

Let's get started!
What's Claude Code?

Until now, Claude could work with files you uploaded or connected. Claude Code is different because it works inside a local project folder on your computer. You build tools with your actual files — scripts and programs that live on your machine, run when you trigger them, and do real work on your data.
Why Claude Code

A regular Claude chat is for conversation — you ask, it answers, and anything it says lives in the chat. An Artifact is for interactive tools that others can use through a link.

Claude Code is a best fit for tools that need to:

• Read files on your machine: CSVs, folders of documents, and exports from other systems.
  • Run actual scripts: Python, shell commands, anything that processes data.
  • Produce real output files: Word documents, spreadsheets, anything that lives on disk.
  • Stitch multiple steps together: read from sources, transform, format, write output.
When the work involves your local files and produces a real deliverable, Claude Code is the best choice.
Scenario: A Tool for Your Task

Imagine this: you run a small consulting practice with two retainer clients. Once a month, each client gets a status report — your formal summary of the past month's work. You've been producing these reports the same way for 9 months. Each one takes about 90 minutes.

You're going on vacation in three weeks. Your colleague Sarah will cover both clients while you're away. Two reports are due during that time.

Sarah is competent, but she doesn't know your format, your sources, or the months of context behind these clients. If she produces the reports from scratch, the clients will notice the difference.

You're going to build her a tool.
Why These Reports Take 90 Minutes
The data isn't in one place. Producing the report means cross-referencing across three sources:

blocks.text: The Acceptance Criterion

You have 9 months of these reports in a folder. Each one was produced by you, by hand. You know what a correct report looks like, because you wrote them.

That's your verification standard. The tool's first real test is running it against last month's inputs. The output should match the report you actually sent.
Running It on Last Month's Data

You run the tool. It produces a Word document. You open it next to last month's actual report and read them side by side.

You'll find three kinds of things:

• Matches — sections the tool produced that look like what you wrote
  • Misses — things the tool didn't catch that you did
  • Surprises — things the tool surfaced that you missed manually (rare but useful)
The misses are the iteration material. Don't fix the code — describe the miss to Claude, and let it iterate the tool.

After Claude builds the first version of the tool, the most useful next step is comparing what you described in the spec against what Claude built. Ask Claude to walk through what it built, step by step, in plain language. Then check each step against three questions:
  • Did anything from the spec get skipped? Something you asked for that isn't in the build.
  • Did Claude add steps you didn't ask for? Sometimes useful, sometimes scope creep.
  • Did Claude interpret a step differently than you meant? The most common gap — the spec said "read every meeting note," Claude built "read meeting notes from this folder, but skip ones older than 30 days."
blocks.title: 💡 Compare What You Asked For to What You Got

blocks.text: How the Iteration Loop Works
When the tool's output doesn't match the reference, the loop is:

• Describe what's wrong, naming the specific case where it appears.
  • Let Claude rebuild the broken piece.
  • Re-run on the same test data.
  • Compare the new output to the reference again.
You repeat until the output matches. Each pass narrows the gap.
The Limits of Vibe Coding
Not everything that could be a tool should be a vibe-coded tool. Three categories of work fit:

• Buildable via vibe coding: recurring work with clear inputs, clear logic, deterministic outputs. The client report tool fits.
  • Requires developer assistance: anything that needs security review, runs on production systems, handles sensitive customer data, or needs to scale beyond your machine.
  • Not suitable for automation at all: work where the judgment changes each time, where the inputs aren't stable, or where the value is in the human doing the thinking.
Knowing which bucket a tool falls into is the most important calibration in vibe coding. Over-scoping into the wrong bucket is how Claude Code projects get abandoned.

  • Iterate by description, not by code. Describe the miss, name the case, let Claude rebuild that piece.
  • Compare the spec to what got built. Gaps, additions, and drift are where the build deviated from the brief.
  • Not every recurring task is the best fit for vibe coding. Stable rules and deterministic outputs fit; judgment-heavy, customer-facing, or production work doesn't.

blocks.text: Build the Tool That Does Your Work

You've been configuring Claude, building Artifacts, and shaping how every conversation starts. Now you'll take a different step — building a real, working tool on your computer that handles a piece of your professional work end to end. A script you run when you need it, that takes inputs and produces a finished deliverable.

That's what Claude Code is for. By the end of this lesson, you'll have a working tool, and you'll know the limits of what's worth building this way. 

Let's get started!
What's Claude Code?

Until now, Claude could work with files you uploaded or connected. Claude Code is different because it works inside a local project folder on your computer. You build tools with your actual files — scripts and programs that live on your machine, run when you trigger them, and do real work on your data.
Why Claude Code

A regular Claude chat is for conversation — you ask, it answers, and anything it says lives in the chat. An Artifact is for interactive tools that others can use through a link.

Claude Code is a best fit for tools that need to:

• Read files on your machine: CSVs, folders of documents, and exports from other systems.
  • Run actual scripts: Python, shell commands, anything that processes data.
  • Produce real output files: Word documents, spreadsheets, anything that lives on disk.
  • Stitch multiple steps together: read from sources, transform, format, write output.
When the work involves your local files and produces a real deliverable, Claude Code is the best choice.
Scenario: A Tool for Your Task

Imagine this: you run a small consulting practice with two retainer clients. Once a month, each client gets a status report — your formal summary of the past month's work. You've been producing these reports the same way for 9 months. Each one takes about 90 minutes.

You're going on vacation in three weeks. Your colleague Sarah will cover both clients while you're away. Two reports are due during that time.

Sarah is competent, but she doesn't know your format, your sources, or the months of context behind these clients. If she produces the reports from scratch, the clients will notice the difference.

You're going to build her a tool.
Why These Reports Take 90 Minutes
The data isn't in one place. Producing the report means cross-referencing across three sources:

• A project tracker (CSV) — what got tracked. Status, hours, deliverables completed and pending.
  • A folder of meeting notes — what got discussed. Decisions made, concerns raised, action items.
  • An email thread export — what's still open. Questions awaiting answers, loops yet to close.

The 90 minutes are the cross-referencing work. Each source on its own is incomplete. The tracker doesn't capture the why. The meeting notes capture conversations, but you don't know what made it into the tracker. The email thread surfaces what's open, but doesn't connect to either.
What the Tool Will Do
You give it three inputs:

• The project tracker CSV
  • The path to the meeting notes folder
  • The client's email address (the tool fetches recent threads via the Gmail connector)
It does the cross-referencing work and produces a finished Word document — the kind of report you'd send to the client after a quick proofread.

feedbackCorrect.text: All three describe what the tool needs to do: read from the file system, produce a file on disk, and combine sources from multiple places. Speed isn't really what separates Claude Code from a chat.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Speed isn't really what sets Claude Code apart from a chat. A chat is fast enough for most one-time work, even when there's a lot of it. What changes here is that the work needs to live as a reusable tool. The chat shape doesn't produce that kind of artifact; the Claude Code shape does.

options.label: The output is a Word document saved to disk that someone else picks up later, not a chat response
Claude Code is generally faster than other Claude surfaces, so it's the right choice when you have many reports to produce
The work pulls from multiple sources — local files plus a Gmail connector — and combines them into one deliverable
The tool needs to read a folder of meeting notes from your computer — file-system access that a chat doesn't have

blocks.question: Why is Claude Code the right surface for this tool, rather than a regular Claude chat or an Artifact?

blocks.text: Before Anything, Set Up the Project
Claude Code works inside a folder. Before building anything, you create or choose the folder the tool will work with.
Connecting the Email Source
The project tracker and meeting notes live in your project folder, where Claude Code can read them directly. The email thread is different — it lives in Gmail, and the tool needs a way to reach it.

That's what Connectors are for. Go to Customize and select Connectors. Click "Add" then "Browse connectors," and then choose Gmail. Sign in, authorize the connection, and Gmail becomes a source the tool can read from. The connection happens once, and the tool uses it every time it runs.
Describe What You're Building Before You Prompt

The temptation is to start prompting immediately. The better move is to describe the tool to yourself first — in writing, in your project folder — so when you prompt Claude, you're handing it a real specification.
A clear spec covers four things:

• Goal = what the tool does, in one sentence
  • Inputs = what files, in what format, in what location
  • Processing = what the tool does to the inputs, step by step
  • Output = what comes out, in what format, where it lands
Skipping this is the most common reason vibe-coded tools end up nearly working instead of actually working.

When writing a spec or prompt, you reference files and folders by typing "@" followed by the path. Two things matter:
  • @file_name includes the file's contents in context. For example, @spec.md loads the spec. Use this when Claude needs to read what's in the file.
  • @folder_name/ includes the folder's contents listing. For example, @data/meetings/ shows Claude what files exist in the meetings folder. Use this when Claude needs to know what's there and then read individual files as needed.

blocks.text: First Build, Test Data First
Now you build. The prompt is short because the spec does the heavy lifting.
Permission Modes

As Claude starts building, you'll notice it doesn't just silently write the file. It pauses and asks. That's the default behavior: Manual mode. Claude tells you what it's about to do, and you approve each step. For a first build, this is the right default: you see what's happening and learn what the tool touches as it's being made.
There are other modes for when you don't want to approve every step:

• "Accept edits" runs through small changes without stopping.
  • Plan maps out the work before any file changes.
  • Auto runs straight through with a background safety check.
  • "Bypass permissions" skips all permission checks essentially and lets Claude execute any tool without prompting.

blocks.text: The Acceptance Criterion

You have 9 months of these reports in a folder. Each one was produced by you, by hand. You know what a correct report looks like, because you wrote them.

That's your verification standard. The tool's first real test is running it against last month's inputs. The output should match the report you actually sent.
Running It on Last Month's Data

You run the tool. It produces a Word document. You open it next to last month's actual report and read them side by side.

You'll find three kinds of things:

• Matches — sections the tool produced that look like what you wrote
  • Misses — things the tool didn't catch that you did
  • Surprises — things the tool surfaced that you missed manually (rare but useful)
The misses are the iteration material. Don't fix the code — describe the miss to Claude, and let it iterate the tool.

After Claude builds the first version of the tool, the most useful next step is comparing what you described in the spec against what Claude built. Ask Claude to walk through what it built, step by step, in plain language. Then check each step against three questions:
  • Did anything from the spec get skipped? Something you asked for that isn't in the build.
  • Did Claude add steps you didn't ask for? Sometimes useful, sometimes scope creep.
  • Did Claude interpret a step differently than you meant? The most common gap — the spec said "read every meeting note," Claude built "read meeting notes from this folder, but skip ones older than 30 days."
blocks.title: 💡 Compare What You Asked For to What You Got

screens.title: 💡 Compare What You Asked For to What You Got

blocks.text: How the Iteration Loop Works
When the tool's output doesn't match the reference, the loop is:

• Describe what's wrong, naming the specific case where it appears.
  • Let Claude rebuild the broken piece.
  • Re-run on the same test data.
  • Compare the new output to the reference again.
You repeat until the output matches. Each pass narrows the gap.
The Limits of Vibe Coding
Not everything that could be a tool should be a vibe-coded tool. Three categories of work fit:

• Buildable via vibe coding: recurring work with clear inputs, clear logic, deterministic outputs. The client report tool fits.
  • Requires developer assistance: anything that needs security review, runs on production systems, handles sensitive customer data, or needs to scale beyond your machine.
  • Not suitable for automation at all: work where the judgment changes each time, where the inputs aren't stable, or where the value is in the human doing the thinking.
Knowing which bucket a tool falls into is the most important calibration in vibe coding. Over-scoping into the wrong bucket is how Claude Code projects get abandoned.

feedbackCorrect.text: Right. Stable rules, clear inputs, deterministic output. The categorization logic is your team's rules, written down — Claude Code can implement them faithfully. Classic vibe-coding territory.

feedbackIncorrect.text: This doesn't need developer help: there's no production system, no customer-facing risk, no need to scale beyond your machine. The rules are explicit, and the inputs are stable. Vibe coding fits cleanly.

blocks.question: A tool that pulls expense receipts from a folder and categorizes them by your team's budget rules

blocks.text:
A tool without documentation is a tool only you can use — because you remember the inputs, the order, and the quirks. Sarah doesn't.

Good tool documentation answers four questions for someone who's never seen it: what does it do, what inputs does it need, how do I run it, and what do I do with the output.
blocks.title: 💡 Why Documentation Matters

blocks.text: The standard place to write good documentation is a file called README.md, saved in your project folder. When anyone opens a tool they've never seen before, the README is the first thing they look for — that's the whole job of the file.

This is a documentation example for a different tool — read it as if you're about to use it for the first time: "Tool: expense-categorize. Usage: run the script with your expense data. Output: a categorized version. Edge cases handled." You'd immediately hit the questions this documentation doesn't answer:

• Where does your data go?
  • What format?
  • What command?
  • What's "a categorized version" — a file, a printed table, a chat response?

Documentation that doesn't survive a stranger's reading isn't ready for a team handoff. Picture the failure: Sarah opens the documentation and can't figure out where to put her data or which command to run, and then ends up texting you from the airport.

Want me to also add a troubleshooting section for the common edge cases?

blocks.text: Handing the Tool to Sarah

The tool lives on your computer. To make it Sarah's tool during your vacation, you need to get the project folder onto her computer.

The simplest way is to zip the whole project folder and send it to her. She unzips it on her machine, opens the folder in Claude Code, and the tool is ready to run. Because the tool uses relative paths, it works wherever she puts the folder.
How Sarah Uses It Each Month

From here on, generating a new client report is straightforward — for you or for Sarah. Drop the new month's inputs into the data folder (or, for your colleagues, into a copy of the folder). Then open the tool's interface, set the client name and the month in the Run panel, and click Generate report. That's it!
The Tool Is Done

You have a working tool. You've verified it against 9 months of reference reports. You've documented it for Sarah. The hard work is over.

What's left is the small habit of running the tool yourself once before vacation — on this month's data, with this month's inputs — to confirm everything's working in your absence. If anything looks off, you fix it now. By the time Sarah's covering, the tool is solid.
A quick note: If you've never used Claude Code before, there's a separate course that walks through the installation, the desktop app, and the core workflows for vibe coding and automations.

• Claude Code earns its place when work needs local files, real scripts, and deliverables on disk. Not chat-shaped, not browser-shaped.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

You've built a tool that turns a 90-minute recurring report process into a faster, reviewable workflow. Sarah can run it. In the next lesson, you'll meet Cowork — the layer that wraps automation around tools like this one. The same client report tool can become part of a larger workflow that runs without anyone triggering it. Let's keep going!
Hand Off the Whole Task

So far, you've been working with Claude in a conversation: describing what you need, reviewing the response, and refining the next request.

Cowork changes that rhythm. Instead of guiding Claude through every step, you describe the outcome you need and let Claude plan and execute the multi-step work. You can follow its progress, step in when needed, or return when the deliverable is ready.

That's what Cowork is for. Let's get started!
What's Cowork?

Claude Cowork is Claude's agentic mode for complex, multi-step work. You describe the outcome you need, and Claude plans the task, breaks the work into steps, uses the tools you have enabled, and produces a finished deliverable. Cowork is available on paid Claude plans. You can use it on desktop, web, and mobile, although web and mobile access may still be rolling out to your plan. The desktop app offers the fullest experience. It's required when Cowork needs to reach local files, your browser, or apps on your computer.
Three things make Cowork particularly useful:

• Extended execution: Claude can work through a multi-step task without waiting for you to prompt every individual step.
  • Multiple sources and tools: A task can combine connected services, web research, project knowledge, and, on desktop, local files or applications.
  • Work that follows you: Remote sessions can continue when you close your laptop, and you can check or steer the same task from desktop, web, or mobile.
Regular chat is still a multi-turn conversation. The difference is that in chat, you usually drive the exchange. In Cowork, you delegate a larger piece of work and supervise the process.
How Cowork Fits With Everything Else
You've now seen several shapes of Claude:

• Regular chat — conversation. You ask, it answers.
  • Connectors — Claude reaching into your tools to read and act.
  • Artifacts — interactive tools that live in a browser and can be shared as a link.
  • Claude Code — a tool for agentic technical and development work.
  • Cowork — autonomous execution of multi-step work across surfaces.
Cowork is especially useful when the task has several steps, draws from multiple sources, and should end in a concrete deliverable.
Judgment Comes First

Before learning how to use Cowork, the first skill is knowing when to use it — and when not to. Cowork is powerful because it can execute across your tools, files, and apps. That same power is what makes the wrong delegation risky. A task assigned to Cowork that shouldn't have been delegated can cause damage. The starting framework is three tiers, based on how much human judgment the work requires.
The Three Tiers of Delegation

Tier 1: Cowork prepares autonomously Use Cowork for low-risk work that mainly involves reading, organizing, or summarizing information. Examples: creating a weekly brief, summarizing project updates, organizing files, or comparing information for your own review. Claude can prepare the result on its own. You still check it before using it.
Tier 2: Cowork prepares, you review before action Use it when Claude can do most of the work, but the final action affects another person or system.

Examples: drafting email replies, suggesting calendar changes, preparing a message for your team, or recommending which tasks to prioritize. Claude prepares the work. You review it and decide what happens next.
Tier 3: Don't delegate Use extra caution when a task is sensitive, difficult to undo, or could affect other people.

Examples: sending messages in your name, making a purchase, deleting important files, changing critical records, or working with sensitive HR, legal, medical, or financial information. Keep Cowork in Manual mode, limit what it can access, and stay close to the task. For some tasks, the safest decision is not to delegate them.

feedbackCorrect.text: The tier framework matters because Cowork can act across your tools and files, and that reach is what makes the wrong delegation costly. Knowing which tier a task belongs to is the first step before deciding whether to use Cowork. Tiers are a framework you use when deciding what to delegate.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Cowork doesn't read the tiers as priority signals. The tiers exist for you, not for Cowork. They're how you decide whether a task should be delegated at all, and how much human review the output needs before it goes anywhere. The judgment lives with you.

options.label: The tiers help Cowork understand what to prioritize when it runs your tasks
Cowork's power across tools is also what makes the wrong delegation risky
The tier of a task determines whether you should use Cowork at all, before you even start writing the task brief

blocks.text: Scenario: Weekly Brief

Imagine you run a small architecture studio with four people on your team. Across any given week, work happens across email, Slack, your project tracker, and your calendar.

Right now, Monday mornings start slowly. You sit down, figuring out what the week holds:

• Which meetings need real prep
  • Which decisions need to come out of you this week
  • Which projects are about to hit a deadline
You piece it together, often catching things later than you'd like.
What the Monday Brief Will Contain

You're going to set up a Cowork task that runs on Sunday evening and already has your whole next week planned.

Your plan will include the five sections, all forward-looking:

• Your week ahead
  • What needs your response or decision this week
  • Ongoing projects status
  • Where your team needs you
  • Top priorities
Let's build your automation step by step.
Where Cowork Lives

Chat and Cowork live in the same Claude workspace. Select Cowork near the message box. Then describe the task you want Claude to complete. Switch back to Chat when you want a regular conversation. You'll need the desktop app if Cowork has to use local folders, Chrome, or apps on your computer.
Working in a Project

A project gives related tasks one shared workspace. Instead of explaining the same task at the beginning of each week, you create a project and tell Claude what it should do. 

For your architecture studio, the project will prepare the same weekly brief using fresh information each time.
Setting Up the Project
For your weekly brief, select Create new project. You only need two things to get started:

• Name — a clear title for the project
  • Description — a short explanation of what the project is for and what Claude should produce
Then select Create project. One thing to know: the name and description help you organize the project, but Claude doesn't use them as task instructions.
What a Project Actually Adds

A project is a reusable context, not the task itself. What matters are the project's instructions and files. They hold information that stays useful from one task to the next, such as your role, team, preferred format, or reference material. You can also add a local folder through the desktop app when the task needs files stored on your computer.
The Three Layers of a Task
A recurring task has three separate parts:

• Project context — what stays the same
  • Connectors — what Claude can access
  • Task message — what Claude should do now
These parts work together, but they do different jobs.
Connecting the Tools Cowork Reads

Before the task runs, the four sources need to be reachable. Cowork uses the same connectors you set up in the first lesson — they authorize once at the account level and are available across surfaces. For your weekly prep, four connectors need to be active:

• Gmail — for the email thread synthesis
  • Slack — for team channel reading
  • Asana — for project status
  • Google Calendar — for the week ahead
Setting Up the Task
Writing a Cowork task is a short conversation, not a long prompt:

• Describe the outcome. Type the task brief in the input field: outcome, sources, scope, and schedule if needed.
  • Review Claude's plan. Before doing anything, Cowork proposes how it'll approach the work. You read the plan, ask for changes if it's off, and approve when it's right.
  • Let it run. Once approved, Cowork executes on its own. You can step away, work on something else, or close the active conversation. The work continues in the background as long as the app stays open.
Three Permission Modes
Before you write the task, one more setting to know about: permission modes. Cowork gives you three levels of control:

• "Manually approve" asks before actions that need approval.
  • "Automatically approve" keeps working while checking actions for safety.
  • "Skip all approvals" continues without asking or using the Auto safety check.

For your first run, stay in "Manually approve." Watch what Cowork pauses on, what it touches, and where it asks for permission. 

Now that the setup is in place, it's time to write the task itself.

blocks.text: Review More Than the File

A polished brief doesn't always mean the task ran well.

Check the visible activity too:

• Which connectors appeared
  • Which sources Claude used
  • Where it asked for permission
  • Whether the task became broader than expected
This helps you review the run, but it is not a complete security audit.
Now Schedule Your Task

You've built a working Cowork task — a project that holds context, a brief that scopes what Cowork reads, and a clean first run you've audited. One step left: turn it into a weekly habit. In the same task, type /schedule, and Claude walks you through cadence options — hourly, daily, weekly, weekdays, or manual. Pick weekly, Sunday 9 p.m., and Cowork saves the schedule. You can find your task (and edit) under Scheduled in the left sidebar.
Your First Run
After your first run, both files appear:

• The document — a week-prep-1 saved in your designated folder
  • The run itself — the Cowork session for this task, showing the full execution

You open the brief first. The five sections are there. The top priorities are right — they read like what you would have written if you'd done the brief yourself. Then — the run. This is how you stay in control of an agentic task. It shows what Cowork read, what it produced, and any steps where it paused or hit something unexpected.

feedbackCorrect.text: The document only shows the end result. The visible activity — which connectors appeared, which sources Claude read, and where it paused for permission — is what tells you how it got there. A brief can read perfectly and still have pulled from a source it shouldn't have, so this check catches scope creep before you repeat or share the workflow.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A clean result doesn't prove a clean process. Cowork could have reached a source you didn't intend, and the document wouldn't show it on its own. Check the visible activity — sources, actions, and permission requests — before repeating or sharing the run.

options.label: The visible sources, actions, and permission requests from the task
Whether the document can be sent automatically next week
Nothing — a correct document proves the whole workflow worked well

blocks.text: Remote Doesn't Mean Risk-Free
A scheduled task using cloud connectors can run while your computer is offline.
That's useful for weekly briefs and reports, but it also means you may not be watching while Claude works.
The less supervision a task has, the more important narrow access and clear boundaries become.
When Sensitive Information Appears
The task runs again next week.
You open the brief and find something that shouldn't be there: a summary of a private HR conversation about a team member's performance.
The information came from a private Slack channel and should never have appeared in a document you might share.

feedbackCorrect.text: The project did not provide Slack access. The connector did. The task guided Claude toward certain sources, but the connected account could still reach more information than the workflow needed.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Neither the project nor the schedule expands Slack permissions. The problem was broad instructions combined with too much connector access.

options.label: The weekly schedule gave Cowork extra Slack permissions
The task was too broad, and the connected Slack account could access the private channel
Adding the project automatically connected every Slack channel

blocks.question: Why did the HR conversation most likely appear?

blocks.text: Instructions Aren't Permissions
"Use only #studio-general" is an instruction, not an access rule.
It helps Claude focus, but it doesn't remove access to other channels your account can reach.
Sensitive work needs two layers of protection:

content.value: Scenario: Weekly Brief

Imagine you run a small architecture studio with four people on your team. Across any given week, work happens across email, Slack, your project tracker, and your calendar.

Right now, Monday mornings start slowly. You sit down, figuring out what the week holds:

• Which meetings need real prep
  • Which decisions need to come out of you this week
  • Which projects are about to hit a deadline
You piece it together, often catching things later than you'd like.
https://d2h7i1o4snhir4.cloudfront.net/page-fragments/de029497-42db-4d94-9034-2327acb90154.webp
What the Monday Brief Will Contain

You're going to set up a Cowork task that runs on Sunday evening and already has your whole next week planned.

• Your week ahead

  • Ongoing projects status
  • Where your team needs you
  • Top priorities
Let's build your automation step by step.

A project gives related tasks one shared workspace. Instead of explaining the same task at the beginning of each week, you create a project and tell Claude what it should do. 

For your architecture studio, the project will prepare the same weekly brief using fresh information each time.

• Name — a clear title for the project

Then select Create project. One thing to know: the name and description help you organize the project, but Claude doesn't use them as task instructions.

You can also add a local folder through the desktop app when the task needs files stored on your computer.

A recurring task has three separate parts:

• Project context — what stays the same
  • Connectors — what Claude can access
  • Task message — what Claude should do now
These parts work together, but they do different jobs.
https://d2h7i1o4snhir4.cloudfront.net/page-fragments/a9aa2a24-3d66-469b-8e82-c054f55d7e45.webp
Connecting the Tools Cowork Reads

Before the task runs, the four sources need to be reachable. Cowork uses the same connectors you set up in the first lesson — they authorize once at the account level and are available across surfaces. For your weekly prep, four connectors need to be active:

• Gmail — for the email thread synthesis
  • Slack — for team channel reading
  • Asana — for project status
  • Google Calendar — for the week ahead
https://d2h7i1o4snhir4.cloudfront.net/page-fragments/a6193545-ab9e-4155-986b-1b0bbd15364a.webp

Writing a Cowork task is a short conversation, not a long prompt:

• Describe the outcome. Type the task brief in the input field: outcome, sources, scope, and schedule if needed.
  • Review Claude's plan. Before doing anything, Cowork proposes how it'll approach the work. You read the plan, ask for changes if it's off, and approve when it's right.
  • Let it run. Once approved, Cowork executes on its own. You can step away, work on something else, or close the active conversation. The work continues in the background as long as the app stays open.

Before you write the task, one more setting to know about: permission modes. Cowork gives you three levels of control:

• "Manually approve" asks before actions that need approval.
  • "Automatically approve" keeps working while checking actions for safety.
  • "Skip all approvals" continues without asking or using the Auto safety check.

For your first run, stay in "Manually approve." Watch what Cowork pauses on, what it touches, and where it asks for permission. 

Now that the setup is in place, it's time to write the task itself.

content.value: Review More Than the File

A polished brief doesn't always mean the task ran well.

Check the visible activity too:

• Which connectors appeared
  • Which sources Claude used
  • Where it asked for permission
  • Whether the task became broader than expected

Now Schedule Your Task

You've built a working Cowork task — a project that holds context, a brief that scopes what Cowork reads, and a clean first run you've audited. One step left: turn it into a weekly habit. Your First Run
After your first run, both files appear:

• The document — a week-prep-1 saved in your designated folder
  • The run itself — the Cowork session for this task, showing the full execution

This is how you stay in control of an agentic task. It shows what Cowork read, what it produced, and any steps where it paused or hit something unexpected.

feedback_incorrect.text: A clean result doesn't prove a clean process. Cowork could have reached a source you didn't intend, and the document wouldn't show it on its own. Check the visible activity — sources, actions, and permission requests — before repeating or sharing the run.

content.value: Remote Doesn't Mean Risk-Free
A scheduled task using cloud connectors can run while your computer is offline.
That's useful for weekly briefs and reports, but it also means you may not be watching while Claude works.
The less supervision a task has, the more important narrow access and clear boundaries become.

The task runs again next week.
You open the brief and find something that shouldn't be there: a summary of a private HR conversation about a team member's performance.
The information came from a private Slack channel and should never have appeared in a document you might share.

feedback_correct.text: The project did not provide Slack access. The connector did. The task guided Claude toward certain sources, but the connected account could still reach more information than the workflow needed.

feedback_incorrect.text: Neither the project nor the schedule expands Slack permissions. The problem was broad instructions combined with too much connector access.

It helps Claude focus, but it doesn't remove access to other channels your account can reach.
Sensitive work needs two layers of protection:

• Clear, narrow instructions
  • Limited account and connector access
