blocks.text: From Brief to Running System

Both layers built. You test the system against a sample batch of five opt-ins from your CSV. The system is ready. Each week, the Claude Code drafter runs against the new opt-ins. Cowork reads what it wrote and sends Day 0 immediately; Day 7 and Day 14 follow on schedule. You don't touch the emails after the initial test — the system handles itself.

What was an hour of weekly manual personalization is now a system that runs without you.
Stepping Back

The talk's three weeks out. The whole workflow happened in Claude: reasoning in chat, visual work in Claude Design, production handoff in Claude Code, and recurring work in Cowork. Each layer did what it was best at; the orchestration focused on ensuring the outputs integrated.

feedbackCorrect.text: Three observations, three real lessons: where integration fails, when automation earns its place, and how reasoning feeds production. The wrong option is the trap — parallel work without handoffs produces four artifacts that don't fit together. Orchestration lives in the handoffs, not in maximizing parallelism.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Parallel-from-the-start sounds efficient, but the handoffs are what make the work integrate. The framework feeds the deck, the deck feeds the page, the page feeds the email sequence. Skip the handoffs and you get four good pieces that don't compose.

options.label: Run all four layers in parallel from the start, because that's the fastest path
Build small automations when the friction shows up, not when you predict it
The deck-to-page handoff is where things can break. Lock the design system first, not last
Reasoning has to finish before production starts, and in a format that production can use

blocks.question: Looking back at the full execution, which observations are the most useful for designing the next workflow like this one?

blocks.text:
Not every project needs all four execution layers. Single-tool work is fine when the deliverable is one artifact. Where the full stack is worth the orchestration overhead:
  • Multi-component projects — anything that produces more than one connected artifact
  • Reasoning + production splits — when the thinking work has to finish before the visual or code work begins
  • Recurring tail — when part of the work continues after the main deliverable ships (the email sequence, the page that lives on)
  • Stakes that justify integration discipline — when the cost of incoherent deliverables is high enough to be worth catching
blocks.title: 💡 When the Full Stack Earns Its Place

blocks.text:
• Orchestration is the integration skill. Not using each tool well, but making sure their outputs fit together at the handoffs.
  • Integration failures live at the seams. The deck and the page can both be correct and still drift from each other; the design system is what carries identity across them.
  • The four-field structure works on real failures the same way it works on predicted ones. Where, what broke and why, the prevention, the verification.
  • Reasoning layers finish before production layers begin. The reasoning's outputs have to be in a format the production layers can use, which is what the structured outline and the audience research were for.
  • Automations earn their place during execution, not before. Wait for the recurring manual step to make itself obvious; then build the small tool.
  • The orchestration is in the handoffs and the sequencing. Not in running things in parallel or in maximizing any one tool's capability.
blocks.title: Key Takeaways

blocks.text: What's Next?

You've now executed a full multi-layer workflow end-to-end. You've seen what handoffs look like in practice, where integration failures live, how to recover from them, and where automation earns its place.

The next lesson moves from one project to a recurring system. You'll see how the same orchestration skill applies to running a small business or a team with Claude as the operating layer — not for a one-time event like a talk, but for ongoing work that compounds week over week.

Let's keep going!

content.value: When Integration Fails

You walk through the page side by side with the deck and notice something off. The deck's accent color appears on the page, but it's slightly different — a touch warmer, less saturated. Typography and spacing match, but the accent color is not quite the same.

This is an integration failure, and now you'll fix it.
The Four-Field Failure Analysis
For any execution-time failure, the analysis structure stays the same:

• Where it occurs — which handoff
  • What broke and why — the specific mechanism of failure
  • Preventive measure — what you'd add to prevent the failure
  • Verification — how you'd confirm the prevention worked
The accent color drift fits the structure cleanly:

• The handoff is from the deck to the page.
  • The mechanism is that the design system extraction captured the color as a description rather than as a locked token.
  • The preventive measure is to lock the color as a hex token in the design system.
  • The verification is a side-by-side check of the accent color across both artifacts.

With the page live and opt-ins coming in, the email sequence has to run. Three emails per opt-in:

  • Day 7: A follow-up referencing the talk and pointing to the recording. Light personalization — name only.
  • Day 14: A deeper-cut email pointing to the article. Templated.

Day 7 and Day 14 are straightforward — Cowork can send them on schedule from a template. The Day 0 welcome is harder. Each one needs personalization that references the visitor's specific opt-in path. 

The orchestration move: have Claude Code generate the personalized welcome drafts, and have Cowork send them along with the templated follow-ups.

question.text: Looking back at the full execution, which observations are the most useful for designing the next workflow like this one?

content.text:
Not every project needs all four execution layers. Single-tool work is fine when the deliverable is one artifact. Where the full stack is worth the orchestration overhead:
  • Multi-component projects — anything that produces more than one connected artifact
  • Reasoning + production splits — when the thinking work has to finish before the visual or code work begins
  • Recurring tail — when part of the work continues after the main deliverable ships (the email sequence, the page that lives on)
  • Stakes that justify integration discipline — when the cost of incoherent deliverables is high enough to be worth catching
content.title: 💡 When the Full Stack Earns Its Place

content.text:
• Orchestration is the integration skill. Not using each tool well, but making sure their outputs fit together at the handoffs.
  • Integration failures live at the seams. The deck and the page can both be correct and still drift from each other; the design system is what carries identity across them.
  • The four-field structure works on real failures the same way it works on predicted ones. Where, what broke and why, the prevention, the verification.
  • Reasoning layers finish before production layers begin. The reasoning's outputs have to be in a format the production layers can use, which is what the structured outline and the audience research were for.
  • Automations earn their place during execution, not before. Wait for the recurring manual step to make itself obvious; then build the small tool.
  • The orchestration is in the handoffs and the sequencing. Not in running things in parallel or in maximizing any one tool's capability.

blocks.text: Executing Across Three Layers

You designed the workflow in the last lesson. You did the reasoning work — the framework and the audience research. 

Now it's time to orchestrate the production. Three Claude surfaces will be working together to ship the project. Claude Design handles the visual work, Claude Code builds the production page and the small automation, and Cowork runs the recurring email sequence. Chat threads through all of it for the reasoning that keeps the work coherent.

By the end of this lesson, the whole stack is in motion.

Let's get started!
What's Orchestration?
Orchestration is the skill of moving work across multiple surfaces so the outputs integrate. Each tool you've learned can produce strong work on its own.

• Claude Design can make a beautiful deck.
  • Claude Code can ship a working page.
  • Claude Cowork can run a recurring task without you.
But put them in sequence, and the question isn't whether each one works — it's whether what they produce fits together.

A workflow can be well-designed and still produce an incoherent deliverable. Each stage on its own can produce a decent result, but the assembly may not work at the handoffs. Orchestration is the work of catching these integration failures.
Scenario: The Conference Talk

You ended last lesson with two outputs in hand: the framework outline (developed in chat with Thinking + Research), and the audience research bundle (produced by Cowork).

  • The companion page

You'll move through them in the following order:

1. Deck, the project's center of gravity.
  2. The page, which extends the deck's design.
  3. The article and email sequence, which extend the page's reach.

The framework outline you developed lives as text — a structured document with the central argument, the three case studies, and the sequence.   • Stakes that justify integration discipline — when the cost of incoherent deliverables is high enough to be worth catching

blocks.text:
• Orchestration is the integration skill. Not using each tool well, but making sure their outputs fit together at the handoffs.
  • Integration failures live at the seams. The deck and the page can both be correct and still drift from each other; the design system is what carries identity across them.
  • The four-field structure works on real failures the same way it works on predicted ones. Where, what broke and why, the prevention, the verification.
  • Reasoning layers finish before production layers begin. The reasoning's outputs have to be in a format the production layers can use, which is what the structured outline and the audience research were for.
  • Automations earn their place during execution, not before. Wait for the recurring manual step to make itself obvious; then build the small tool.
  • The orchestration is in the handoffs and the sequencing. Not in running things in parallel or in maximizing any one tool's capability.

blocks.text: What's Next?

You've now executed a full multi-layer workflow end-to-end. You've seen what handoffs look like in practice, where integration failures live, how to recover from them, and where automation earns its place.

The next lesson moves from one project to a recurring system. You'll see how the same orchestration skill applies to running a small business or a team with Claude as the operating layer — not for a one-time event like a talk, but for ongoing work that compounds week over week.

Let's keep going!
Claude for Small Business

Every small business owner has a list of operational work that piles up after hours: month-end close, invoice chasing, campaign planning, the briefings nobody has time to write.

Claude for Small Business is built for exactly that work — a plugin with 30+ ready-to-run skills wired into the tools you already pay for. This lesson teaches you to configure them, run them safely, and build the governance layer that makes them deployable in a real business.

Let's get started!
What's Claude for Small Business?

Claude for Small Business is a plugin. It's not a new product or a separate subscription. It runs on whatever paid Claude plan you already have.

What the plugin adds:

• 30+ ready-to-run skills
  • 11 connectors that bring data from the platforms you already pay for
How to Set Everything Up
Setup is simple. Go to Customize and choose Plugins. Search "Small Business" and click "+". You added the plugin.
The Skills
The skills span the operational work small business owners actually do:

• Finance: payroll planning, month-end close, cash-flow forecasting, tax-season prep, margin analysis
  • Sales and marketing: lead triage, campaign planning, customer pulse reports
  • Operations: invoice chasing, contract routing, business briefings
  • Customer service: support triage, response drafting
Each one is calibrated for a real recurring task. The skill knows what to do; you tell it the specifics for your business.

The Small Business plugin works in both Chat and Cowork, but the experience is different.
  • In Chat, commands like /monday-brief run on demand: Claude pulls from your connectors and shows the result in the conversation, but can't save to your desktop or run on its own
  • In Cowork, the same commands become hands-off workflows. Briefs save directly to your local folders and can run on a schedule — like your Monday Brief landing on your Desktop at 7 a.m. before you've opened the app.
Rule of thumb: use Chat to run a check right now; use Cowork to make it a weekly ritual.

blocks.text: Two ways to run a skill inside Cowork:

• Type a slash command — every skill has one. For example, /plan-payroll opens the payroll planning workflow, /close-month opens the month-end close.
  • Describe what you need in plain language — type "plan payroll for next week" or "close the books for November" into the chat, and Claude routes you to the right skill automatically.
The skill's in four moves:

• Choosing which workflow maps to your highest-friction recurring task
  • Configuring it correctly the first time so the output is usable, not generic
  • Designing the approval boundary — what Claude prepares, what you review, what should never run without sign-off
  • Auditing existing workflows to find the gaps that cause silent failures over time
Each of these gets its focus in this lesson.
Scenario: Your Podcast Studio

Imagine you're a founder of Wavefile Studios, a 6-person podcast production studio. Three years in. You produce 12 active shows for clients — a mix of corporate podcasts, brand-funded shows, and a handful of indie creators on retainer. Your team: 2 producers, 2 audio engineers, 1 account manager, and you.
Your stack:

• QuickBooks for the books
  • PayPal for invoices
  • HubSpot for the client pipeline
  • DocuSign for production contracts
  • Canva for show artwork and social promo
  • Google Workspace for everything else
  • Slack for internal communication
The Operations Problem
You're producing too much yourself:

• Month-end close
  • Invoice chasing
  • Show artwork in Canva
  • Client status reports
Every one of these is a recurring task. And every task is a workflow that Small Business has a prebuilt version of — if you configure them right and put the approval boundary in the right place.

The plugin is installed and ready to use. From there, you connect the tools your studio uses. The plugin's workflows and skills become available as slash commands in any chat — /monday-brief, /month-end-prep, /plan-payroll, and so on. You can type it in a chat or choose from the Plugin panel. To work with all the capabilities, you need to use Connectors. You authorize each connector separately, such as QuickBooks, PayPal, etc. Connect the ones your studio uses. The skill only works with live data once the relevant tool is connected.
Picking the First Workflow

With the plugin installed and the connectors authorized, the first decision is which workflow to start with. The right first workflow is the one that takes the most time and has the lowest risk if Claude gets it slightly wrong. That's almost never an invoice or a contract route. It's usually the Monday brief — read-only, low-stakes, and immediately useful.

The Monday brief pulls your cash position from QuickBooks, incoming settlements from PayPal, pipeline movement from HubSpot, and your calendar from Google Workspace into a single Slack message. It tells you the three things that need your attention today.

feedbackCorrect.text: Low risk, frequent feedback, and habit-building are what make a good first workflow. Time saved isn't the criterion. You want a workflow where you can spot mistakes quickly and where mistakes don't cost you. The morning brief checks all three boxes.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Using the most connectors at once is the opposite of a good first move. You want to verify that each connector works correctly on its own before chaining them. Starting with a workflow that touches everything means you can't isolate the source if something looks off.

options.label: It's read-only — Claude doesn't post, pay, or send anything, so the risk of getting it wrong is contained
It gets you used to reviewing Claude's output as part of your routine, which is the habit every other workflow depends on
It uses the most connectors at once, which exercises the full system
It runs daily, so you see the output quality often enough to catch any drift early

blocks.text: Running Your First Skill — Monday Brief

With QuickBooks, PayPal, HubSpot, Google Calendar, and Slack connected, you run your first skill. In Cowork, you type /monday-brief and hit enter. The skill responds with a quick intake form: where to post the summary (here in chat, in a Slack channel, etc.), and where to save the brief file (Cloud Drive, desktop, etc.). Pick Slack and Cloud Drive, then submit.

Claude pulls your cash position from QuickBooks, incoming settlements from PayPal, pipeline movement from HubSpot, this week's calendar from Google Workspace, and posts a brief summary to your private Slack channel after your approval.

Three things flagged at the top:

• Respond to two aged HubSpot leads
  • Prep the 10 a.m. client review
  • Confirm cash position covers Friday's payroll
The full brief saves to your Drive. A short summary with the flagged items goes to the Slack channel after approval.
A Higher-Stakes Skill — Month-End Prep
With Monday brief running cleanly, you take on a higher-stakes skill: month-end prep. This is the work of closing your books for the month:

• Reconciling what you earned against what your systems show
  • Catching anything that doesn't match
  • Producing a clean record you can hand to your accountant.
You type /month-end-prep in Cowork.
The skill walks you through the close in a conversation. As a result:

• It reconciles your QuickBooks transactions against PayPal settlements.
  • Flags uncategorized transactions and suspicious duplicates.
  • Asks you about any missing receipts it can't find.
  • Exports a close packet — an xlsx with the reconciliation and a one-page PDF you can forward to your accountant.

Unlike the Monday brief (read-only), month-end prep produces an artifact that will reach your accountant. The configuration step matters because of what the output is used for, not just what it contains. When you run /month-end-prep, you'll provide context up front so Claude knows what to flag, what to surface, and what to do when something's ambiguous.
Where to Run the Skill

Open a fresh conversation in Cowork for this — don't reuse the Monday brief thread. Each workflow gets its own focused session. Type /month-end-prep to start. Claude opens the workflow and immediately asks for the setup details. The configuration prompt is how you answer those questions in one pass instead of letting Claude ask them one at a time.

blocks.text: The Review Step

The close packet lands in your Drive — the reconciliation .xlsx file alongside the one-page PDF summary. You open both. Four flagged items: three are routine timing differences, one is a duplicate refund that's already disputed.

You approve and forward it to your accountant.
The Approval Boundary

An important question you might have already thought about: which workflows should run without your approval, and which shouldn't? This is the design question every Small Business setup eventually has to answer. Getting it wrong doesn't just produce bad outputs — in a financial or client-facing context, it produces liability. The framework: three risk tiers, each with its own approval requirement.
The Three Tiers

• Tier 1: Read-only synthesis. Claude reads information and produces something for your reading — a brief, a report, a summary. There's no action step. Suitable for: morning briefs, lead triage summaries, draft research.
  • Tier 2: Action with required approval. Claude prepares work that could result in action (drafts, recommendations, queued sends), then hard-stops. The workflow blocks until you click approve. Suitable for: invoice sends, contract routes, payroll runs, campaign sends.
  • Tier 3: Never automate. Some decisions and the execution both stay manual. Suitable for legal disputes, anything involving sensitive employee or client information.
Each Wavefile workflow gets assigned to a tier.

• The Monday brief is Tier 1 — synthesis, no action.
  • The month-end close is Tier 2 — the result doesn't go to the accountant without your sign-off.
Writing Your Protocol

With the three tiers in mind, you write the protocol for Wavefile — a one-page document that names every active workflow and its tier assignment.

You save it to your Drive, share it with your account manager and producers, and reference it whenever a new workflow gets proposed. The document says: this workflow runs at this tier, with this approval requirement, with this escalation trigger.

Produce a weekly client status report for your reading
Respond to support inquiries about ongoing legal disputes

blocks.text: Stress-Testing the Protocol
The way to find out where the protocol holds is to run real edge cases — situations the original protocol didn't model. Three scenarios worth running:

• A workflow that triggers outside business hours
  • A client with a non-standard approval chain
  • An invoice amount above the protocol's escalation threshold
For each one, your protocol has to specify what happens — and whether it holds or needs to evolve.

feedbackCorrect.text: Two scenarios were handled correctly as-designed; one required a clearly-named variant of an existing tier — not a boundary change. The protocol passed because edge cases were thought through during design, not improvised under pressure.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The temptation is to revise the protocol every time an edge case surfaces — that's exactly what makes protocols feel like obstacles. Some edge cases the protocol handles; some need a named variant; very few require the boundary to move. Knowing which is the skill.

options.label: Off-hours lead — protocol holds (Tier 1 review boundary works as intended)
Above-threshold invoice — protocol holds (escalation trigger fires correctly)
Non-standard approval chain — protocol evolves with a variant (expanded sign-off list, same tier)

blocks.question: Which of the three scenarios required your protocol to change?

blocks.text: When the Prebuilt Skills Don't Cover It

The prebuilt skills handle the most common operational work. They don't handle everything.

When you need a workflow that's not in the prebuilt set, you build it directly in Cowork using the same connectors. The plugin provides you with connectors and example skills, and Cowork lets you compose new workflows from them.

Not every business needs all available workflows. The plugin earns its place when these are all true:
  • You use multiple connector-supported tools. At least 2-3 of QuickBooks, PayPal, HubSpot, DocuSign, Canva, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or Slack.
  • Operational work is consuming meaningful time. Month-end takes days, invoice chasing is constant, and briefings happen ad-hoc.
  • The work follows patterns. The same shape of task happens repeatedly, with variations.
  • You're the bottleneck for review. Work piles up because you're the only one who can approve it.
When these are true, Claude for Small Business takes the operational tail off your plate. When they're not, individual Cowork tasks may be a better fit.

blocks.text: Claude for Small Business

Every small business owner has a list of operational work that piles up after hours: month-end close, invoice chasing, campaign planning, the briefings nobody has time to write.

Claude for Small Business is built for exactly that work — a plugin with 30+ ready-to-run skills wired into the tools you already pay for. This lesson teaches you to configure them, run them safely, and build the governance layer that makes them deployable in a real business.

Let's get started!
What's Claude for Small Business?

Claude for Small Business is a plugin. It's not a new product or a separate subscription. It runs on whatever paid Claude plan you already have.

What the plugin adds:

• 30+ ready-to-run skills
  • 11 connectors that bring data from the platforms you already pay for
How to Set Everything Up
Setup is simple. Go to Customize and choose Plugins. Search "Small Business" and click "+". You added the plugin.
The Skills
The skills span the operational work small business owners actually do:

• Finance: payroll planning, month-end close, cash-flow forecasting, tax-season prep, margin analysis
  • Sales and marketing: lead triage, campaign planning, customer pulse reports
  • Operations: invoice chasing, contract routing, business briefings
  • Customer service: support triage, response drafting
Each one is calibrated for a real recurring task. The skill knows what to do; you tell it the specifics for your business.

The Small Business plugin works in both Chat and Cowork, but the experience is different.
  • In Chat, commands like /monday-brief run on demand: Claude pulls from your connectors and shows the result in the conversation, but can't save to your desktop or run on its own
  • In Cowork, the same commands become hands-off workflows. Briefs save directly to your local folders and can run on a schedule — like your Monday Brief landing on your Desktop at 7 a.m. before you've opened the app.
Rule of thumb: use Chat to run a check right now; use Cowork to make it a weekly ritual.
blocks.title: Chat vs. Cowork

blocks.text: Two ways to run a skill inside Cowork:

• Type a slash command — every skill has one. For example, /plan-payroll opens the payroll planning workflow, /close-month opens the month-end close.
  • Describe what you need in plain language — type "plan payroll for next week" or "close the books for November" into the chat, and Claude routes you to the right skill automatically.
The skill's in four moves:

• Choosing which workflow maps to your highest-friction recurring task
  • Configuring it correctly the first time so the output is usable, not generic
  • Designing the approval boundary — what Claude prepares, what you review, what should never run without sign-off
  • Auditing existing workflows to find the gaps that cause silent failures over time
Each of these gets its focus in this lesson.
Scenario: Your Podcast Studio

Imagine you're a founder of Wavefile Studios, a 6-person podcast production studio. Three years in. You produce 12 active shows for clients — a mix of corporate podcasts, brand-funded shows, and a handful of indie creators on retainer. Your team: 2 producers, 2 audio engineers, 1 account manager, and you.
Your stack:

• QuickBooks for the books
  • PayPal for invoices
  • HubSpot for the client pipeline
  • DocuSign for production contracts
  • Canva for show artwork and social promo
  • Google Workspace for everything else
  • Slack for internal communication
The Operations Problem
You're producing too much yourself:

• Month-end close
  • Invoice chasing
  • Show artwork in Canva
  • Client status reports
Every one of these is a recurring task. And every task is a workflow that Small Business has a prebuilt version of — if you configure them right and put the approval boundary in the right place.

The plugin is installed and ready to use. From there, you connect the tools your studio uses. The plugin's workflows and skills become available as slash commands in any chat — /monday-brief, /month-end-prep, /plan-payroll, and so on. You can type it in a chat or choose from the Plugin panel. To work with all the capabilities, you need to use Connectors. You authorize each connector separately, such as QuickBooks, PayPal, etc. Connect the ones your studio uses. The skill only works with live data once the relevant tool is connected.
Picking the First Workflow

With the plugin installed and the connectors authorized, the first decision is which workflow to start with. The right first workflow is the one that takes the most time and has the lowest risk if Claude gets it slightly wrong. That's almost never an invoice or a contract route. It's usually the Monday brief — read-only, low-stakes, and immediately useful.

The Monday brief pulls your cash position from QuickBooks, incoming settlements from PayPal, pipeline movement from HubSpot, and your calendar from Google Workspace into a single Slack message. It tells you the three things that need your attention today.

feedbackCorrect.text: Low risk, frequent feedback, and habit-building are what make a good first workflow. Time saved isn't the criterion. You want a workflow where you can spot mistakes quickly and where mistakes don't cost you. The morning brief checks all three boxes.

feedbackIncorrect.text: Using the most connectors at once is the opposite of a good first move. You want to verify that each connector works correctly on its own before chaining them. Starting with a workflow that touches everything means you can't isolate the source if something looks off.

options.label: It's read-only — Claude doesn't post, pay, or send anything, so the risk of getting it wrong is contained
It gets you used to reviewing Claude's output as part of your routine, which is the habit every other workflow depends on
It uses the most connectors at once, which exercises the full system
It runs daily, so you see the output quality often enough to catch any drift early

blocks.question: Why is the Monday brief usually the right first workflow to set up, even when other workflows would save more time?

blocks.text: Running Your First Skill — Monday Brief

With QuickBooks, PayPal, HubSpot, Google Calendar, and Slack connected, you run your first skill. In Cowork, you type /monday-brief and hit enter. The skill responds with a quick intake form: where to post the summary (here in chat, in a Slack channel, etc.), and where to save the brief file (Cloud Drive, desktop, etc.). Pick Slack and Cloud Drive, then submit.

Claude pulls your cash position from QuickBooks, incoming settlements from PayPal, pipeline movement from HubSpot, this week's calendar from Google Workspace, and posts a brief summary to your private Slack channel after your approval.

Three things flagged at the top:

• Respond to two aged HubSpot leads
  • Prep the 10 a.m. client review
  • Confirm cash position covers Friday's payroll
The full brief saves to your Drive. A short summary with the flagged items goes to the Slack channel after approval.
A Higher-Stakes Skill — Month-End Prep
With Monday brief running cleanly, you take on a higher-stakes skill: month-end prep. This is the work of closing your books for the month:

• Reconciling what you earned against what your systems show
  • Catching anything that doesn't match
  • Producing a clean record you can hand to your accountant.
You type /month-end-prep in Cowork.
The skill walks you through the close in a conversation. As a result:

• It reconciles your QuickBooks transactions against PayPal settlements.
  • Flags uncategorized transactions and suspicious duplicates.
  • Asks you about any missing receipts it can't find.
  • Exports a close packet — an xlsx with the reconciliation and a one-page PDF you can forward to your accountant.

Unlike the Monday brief (read-only), month-end prep produces an artifact that will reach your accountant. The configuration step matters because of what the output is used for, not just what it contains. When you run /month-end-prep, you'll provide context up front so Claude knows what to flag, what to surface, and what to do when something's ambiguous.
Where to Run the Skill

Open a fresh conversation in Cowork for this — don't reuse the Monday brief thread. Each workflow gets its own focused session. Type /month-end-prep to start. Claude opens the workflow and immediately asks for the setup details. The configuration prompt is how you answer those questions in one pass instead of letting Claude ask them one at a time.

correctTokens: Don't mark the close packet final
blocks.exampleResponse:
Got it. I'll close June 2026 for Wavefile Studios. I'll reconcile QuickBooks transactions with PayPal settlements, flag any mismatches over $50, and pull anything uncategorized or missing a receipt into a separate review list. I'll draft the P&L narrative as a Google Doc you can edit before forwarding. Nothing will be marked final or shared until you approve the full close packet. 

First question: I've pulled four uncategorized transactions from the first week of June (totaling $1,840) into the review list, as you requested. Should I keep going with the reconciliation, and we'll review them together at the end, or pause now to walk through them?
blocks.prompt: Complete the configuration prompt for the month-end close.
blocks.template: I'm closing [month] for my business — Wavefile Studios. [Command] and any uncategorized transaction. [Output requirement]. [Constraint] or share anything until I approve. Walk me through anything that needs my input before the packet is final.
tokens: Don't mark the close packet final

blocks.text: The Review Step

The close packet lands in your Drive — the reconciliation .xlsx file alongside the one-page PDF summary. You open both. Four flagged items: three are routine timing differences, one is a duplicate refund that's already disputed.

You approve and forward it to your accountant.
The Approval Boundary

An important question you might have already thought about: which workflows should run without your approval, and which shouldn't? This is the design question every Small Business setup eventually has to answer. Getting it wrong doesn't just produce bad outputs — in a financial or client-facing context, it produces liability. The framework: three risk tiers, each with its own approval requirement.
The Three Tiers

• Tier 1: Read-only synthesis. Claude reads information and produces something for your reading — a brief, a report, a summary. There's no action step. Suitable for: morning briefs, lead triage summaries, draft research.
  • Tier 2: Action with required approval. Claude prepares work that could result in action (drafts, recommendations, queued sends), then hard-stops. The workflow blocks until you click approve. Suitable for: invoice sends, contract routes, payroll runs, campaign sends.
  • Tier 3: Never automate. Some decisions and the execution both stay manual. Suitable for legal disputes, anything involving sensitive employee or client information.
Each Wavefile workflow gets assigned to a tier.

• The Monday brief is Tier 1 — synthesis, no action.
  • The month-end close is Tier 2 — the result doesn't go to the accountant without your sign-off.
Writing Your Protocol

With the three tiers in mind, you write the protocol for Wavefile — a one-page document that names every active workflow and its tier assignment.

You save it to your Drive, share it with your account manager and producers, and reference it whenever a new workflow gets proposed. The document says: this workflow runs at this tier, with this approval requirement, with this escalation trigger.

pairs.left: Send podcast contract reminders to clients
Produce a weekly client status report for your reading
Respond to support inquiries about ongoing legal disputes

blocks.prompt: For each Wavefile workflow, match the correct risk tier.
blocks.title: Assign the Right Tier

blocks.text: Stress-Testing the Protocol
The way to find out where the protocol holds is to run real edge cases — situations the original protocol didn't model. Three scenarios worth running:

• A workflow that triggers outside business hours
  • A client with a non-standard approval chain
  • An invoice amount above the protocol's escalation threshold
For each one, your protocol has to specify what happens — and whether it holds or needs to evolve.

feedbackCorrect.text: Two scenarios were handled correctly as-designed; one required a clearly-named variant of an existing tier — not a boundary change. The protocol passed because edge cases were thought through during design, not improvised under pressure.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The temptation is to revise the protocol every time an edge case surfaces — that's exactly what makes protocols feel like obstacles. Some edge cases the protocol handles; some need a named variant; very few require the boundary to move. Knowing which is the skill.

options.label: Off-hours lead — protocol holds (Tier 1 review boundary works as intended)
Above-threshold invoice — protocol holds (escalation trigger fires correctly)
Non-standard approval chain — protocol evolves with a variant (expanded sign-off list, same tier)

blocks.question: Which of the three scenarios required your protocol to change?

blocks.text: When the Prebuilt Skills Don't Cover It

The prebuilt skills handle the most common operational work. They don't handle everything.

When you need a workflow that's not in the prebuilt set, you build it directly in Cowork using the same connectors. The plugin provides you with connectors and example skills, and Cowork lets you compose new workflows from them.

Not every business needs all available workflows. The plugin earns its place when these are all true:
  • You use multiple connector-supported tools. At least 2-3 of QuickBooks, PayPal, HubSpot, DocuSign, Canva, Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, or Slack.
  • Operational work is consuming meaningful time. Month-end takes days, invoice chasing is constant, and briefings happen ad-hoc.
  • The work follows patterns. The same shape of task happens repeatedly, with variations.
  • You're the bottleneck for review. Work piles up because you're the only one who can approve it.
When these are true, Claude for Small Business takes the operational tail off your plate. When they're not, individual Cowork tasks may be a better fit.

The next lesson teaches a capability Claude excels at — long-document mastery. You'll learn to process 90+ page documents in a single conversation, compare versions side-by-side, extract structured data from dense prose, and surface contradictions buried across distant sections. Long-Document Mastery

You've made it to the final lesson of this course. Big congrats! You've come a long way — from running your first connector prompt to orchestrating multi-surface workflows.

This last lesson focuses on reasoning across long and complex documents. Claude shines when the task requires extracting structured data, comparing versions side by side, and finding contradictions.

Let's get started!
The Capability Claim

When you bring a large document to a chat with Claude, you're working with large context window. The whole document is in scope at once. Claude can reference page 87 while answering a question about page 12 without losing the context. This is what makes long-document work feel different. The whole document and your questions about it live in the same conversation — no need to break it apart in chunks and feed it piece by piece.
Three Ways to Work With Long Documents
Working with long documents makes three kinds of tasks easier:

• Structured extraction: pulling obligations, dollar amounts, and deadlines, not a narrative summary
  • Version comparison: finding material changes between two versions of the same document, with risk flags
  • Contradiction detection: finding contradicting clauses, the kind of error that hides in plain sight when you read sequentially
These are the skills you'll work through in this lesson.
Scenario: Analyzing a Complex Contract
Imagine this: you've been offered a senior role at a new company. The offer landed in your inbox last night. The package is 95 pages across five files:

• The offer letter itself
  • The equity plan document
  • The company handbook
  • The benefits summary
  • The indemnification agreement
You have a week to respond. Before you sign anything, you need to know exactly what you're agreeing to:

• What gets paid when
  • What's guaranteed vs. conditional
  • What happens if you leave (voluntarily, involuntarily, after acquisition)
  • Where the fine print might contradict the headline terms
Getting the Documents Into the Chat

You upload all five documents into a single chat — the same way you learned for File creation before (drag-and-drop or the attachment menu). Claude reads them as one combined context.

For best results on long-document work, start a fresh chat dedicated to this analysis. Don't add the documents into an existing conversation — keep the context window focused on the work at hand.
Summary vs. Structured Extraction

With the documents loaded, the temptation is to prompt as you would for any document: "Summarize the key terms of this offer." This produces a readable summary. It is useful if you want to understand what's in the document at a high level, but not really when you're making a data-informed decision. A different kind of prompt — a structured extraction prompt — produces actionable data. The difference shows up the moment you try to act on the output.
The Two Prompts, Side by Side

Here are the two prompts for the same offer package: Prompt A — Summary: "Summarize the key terms of this offer letter and equity plan." Prompt B — Structured Extraction: "For every financial commitment in this offer package, extract: the dollar amount, when it pays, whether it's guaranteed or conditional, and what conditions would cancel the payment. Output as a table." Both prompts cover the same material, but they produce different kinds of output: a narrative summary and structured data.

feedbackCorrect.text: Naming the exact fields tells Claude what to look for in every item. Specifying the output format means the result lands in a shape you can use directly. Defining the scope precisely sets the boundaries. The three together turn a vague request into a structured task.

feedbackIncorrect.text: A prompt's length doesn't determine its strength. The three elements that make Prompt B stronger are the named fields, the defined format, and the precise scope. Naming the exact fields tells Claude what to look for in every item. Specifying the output format means the result lands in a shape you can use directly. Defining the scope precisely sets the boundaries.

options.label: It defines the scope precisely, not a loose category like "key terms"
It uses more words, which gives Claude more to work with
It specifies the output format rather than letting Claude choose
It names exactly which fields to extract

blocks.question: What do you think makes Prompt B drive the better output?

blocks.text: The Extraction Pattern
The pattern Prompt B uses works for long-document extraction when the goal is to turn prose into structured data:

• Scope: what set of items you want extracted (every obligation, financial commitment, and deadline)
  • Fields: which attributes to extract for each item (named explicitly)
  • Format: how the output should be structured (table, JSON, structured list)
When all three slots are filled, the output is easier to review, compare, and use.

blocks.exampleResponse: Extracting now. I'll pull every post-termination obligation from the offer package — non-compete, non-solicit, confidentiality, IP assignment, and any other restriction that survives termination. For each one, I'll give you the duration (in months), the geographic scope, the activities restricted, and whether the obligation is reduced if termination is involuntary. Table coming in the next message.
blocks.prompt: Write the prompt for extracting all post-termination obligations from the offer package — anything that binds you after you leave the company.
blocks.template: For every [scope] in this offer package, extract: [field], geographic scope, and activities restricted. Present the output [format].

blocks.text: Version Comparison

With the extraction in hand, you knew what you wanted to push back on — the obligations that were too restrictive and the conditions that needed to be tightened. You shared the extraction with your lawyer and gave them a list of changes to negotiate. A week later, a revised version comes back — same five documents, but with redlines and counter-proposals from your side.

Now you need to know exactly what changed between the two versions: the actual differences — every moved term, added or removed clause, and shifted number. This is where the context window earns its place. Both versions, all five documents each, all loaded at once.
The Comparison Prompt

Comparison prompts have the same structural pattern as extraction prompts, with one addition: you name both versions, and you specify what counts as a meaningful change. The trick: don't ask Claude to find "all differences." That returns formatting noise alongside substantive changes. Instead, name the categories of change that matter and ask for risk flags for changes that contradict your stated priorities.

correctTokens: modified terms, added obligations, removed obligations
blocks.exampleResponse: Comparison complete. I found 23 material changes across the two versions. Most are minor (rephrased clauses, formatting fixes), but 6 are substantive: equity vesting cliff reduced from 12 months to 9 months (favorable), severance reduced from 6 months to 3 months (unfavorable), non-compete geographic scope expanded from "United States" to "global" (significant risk — flagged), IP assignment scope clarified to exclude personal projects (favorable), arbitration clause added requiring all disputes to go through binding arbitration (flagged for legal review), and the bonus structure shifted from guaranteed to discretionary (significant risk — flagged). Full change log in the next message.
blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt to compare the original document (V1) and the revised version (V2). Both are loaded as separate files.
blocks.template: Compare [input] and V2 document. Identify [change categories]. For each change, [command]. Output as a structured change log.
tokens: modified terms, added obligations, removed obligations

blocks.text: Finding Contradictions

Once you trust the comparison, you can use Claude's full-document view to do something harder: find contradictions within the document itself.

Long contracts contradict themselves more often than you can expect. A clause on page 3 grants you a right; a clause on page 58 quietly takes it back. Both clauses can be perfectly written on their own — and incompatible the moment you try to act on them together.
What This Looks Like in Practice

An example from your offer package: the offer letter says you can work on outside projects with approval; the IP assignment clause says all work product belongs to the company. 

Finding these by reading sequentially is hard, but finding them with the document loaded as one context is what Claude can help you with.

correctTokens: cite each contradicting clause by page number
blocks.exampleResponse:
Scanning the full offer package now. I'm looking for clauses that conflict in their actual effect — not just different wording, but provisions that would be impossible to satisfy simultaneously, or that grant rights in one section that another section takes away. 

Three contradictions: 
— The change-of-control acceleration in the equity plan conflicts with the indemnification voiding clause (page 12 vs. page 47).
— The outside projects clause in the offer letter conflicts with the IP assignment scope (page 3 vs. page 58).
— The severance trigger in the offer letter conflicts with the dispute resolution clause's mandatory arbitration (page 4 vs. page 71). 

Each one cited by page number.
blocks.prompt: Complete the prompt to find contradictions across the offer package.
blocks.template: Across all five documents in this offer package, identify any clauses that appear to grant a right or guarantee in one section but limit or void it in another. For each contradiction found, [command]. [Output format].
tokens: cite each contradicting clause by page number

blocks.text: The Attention Drift Problem

Three contradictions found across nearly a hundred pages. But before you trust this output completely, there's one risk worth knowing about: attention drift. When Claude analyzes a long document, the first few sections can get more rigorous treatment than the later ones. The extraction is more thorough, the risk flags more numerous, and the structure more careful. By section 12, the work might be visibly thinner.
What Drift Looks Like
Specific indicators that attention drifted across the document:

• Missing categories: Fields that appear consistently in early sections but stop appearing in later ones.
  • Shorter entries: The same kind of finding gets a one-line treatment late that would have gotten a paragraph early.
  • Absence of risk flags: Flags appear regularly in the first half, then disappear in the second half (when the second half should be no less risky).
  • Generic language: Specific clause references early, vague references late.
  • Skipped subsections: Entire sections of the document not represented in the output.
If you see any two of these in the same analysis, the analysis drifted. The fix is structural.

feedbackCorrect.text: The pattern (consistent quality early, thin output late) is the signature of attention drift, not of genuinely uneven content. Real document content variance produces scattered patterns, not a clean front-loaded one. The fix: chunk the analysis by section and re-run on the later parts, then merge.

feedbackIncorrect.text: The "uneven content" and "prioritization" explanations might be true, but you can't confirm them from the output alone. A clean drop after a certain point is more often attention drift than real content variance, so it's worth verifying before relying on the analysis.

options.label: The later sections genuinely contain fewer items worth flagging — uneven document content is normal
Claude prioritized the most important items and skipped less important ones in the later sections
Attention drift — Claude's analysis thinned across the document, missing items in the later sections

blocks.question: You extracted data from all 95 pages. The first 40 produced 15 detailed entries, including 9 risk flags, while the last 55 produced only 6 entries and no flags. What’s the most likely explanation?

blocks.text: Verification and Chunking

When drift is detected, you verify the analysis by rerunning it on a specific section and comparing the results. The verification prompt is short: "Re-run the same extraction on pages 60 through 95 only. Use the same fields. Output as a table." Compare the new output against what the full-document run produced for those pages. The new output will typically catch entries that the first pass missed.

For documents long enough that drift is likely, you can chunk the work upfront — analyze sections sequentially, then merge. The trade-off: chunking can lose cross-sectional references (contradiction-finding becomes harder). So the decision of when to chunk matters.
When to Chunk vs. Process in Full
Document length is only part of the decision. The other part is cross-reference density — how much one section depends on another. Three quick rules:

• If short and reference-dense (under 30 pages with heavy cross-references), process in full, no chunking.
  • If long and reference-light (sections are mostly independent of each other), chunk by section.
  • If long and reference-dense (over 50 pages, sections refer to each other constantly), process in full first, then verify by re-running on later sections.

pairs.left: A 20-page employment contract with frequent cross-references
A 150-page company handbook with independent sections
A 90-page acquisition agreement where every clause depends on document definitions
pairs.right: Process in full, then verify by re-running on later sections

blocks.prompt: For each document, match the right approach.
blocks.title: Decide the Approach

blocks.text: When Long-Document Mastery Earns Its Place
Not every document needs this treatment. Single-page memos don't. Documents you'll skim once and discard don't. Where this skill earns its place:

• Documents you're committing to: contracts, agreements, terms you'll be bound by
  • Documents with money attached: financial commitments hidden across narrative prose
  • Documents you'll need to reference later: extracting once, referring back many times
  • Documents that come in versions: anything where the comparison work matters as much as the content
When any of these is true, the extraction–comparison–verification pattern is often more reliable than reading the document from start to finish.

• Structured prompts usually produce clearer, more focused results than general ones. Name the scope, the fields, and the format.
  • Comparison work is its own skill. Name both versions, name what counts as a meaningful change, and ask for risk flags.
  • Contradictions hide in cross-references. Clauses that look fine alone can be incompatible together; the context window lets Claude find them.
  • Attention can drift across long documents. Missing categories, shorter entries, vanishing risk flags are the signals.
  • Chunking trades cross-section visibility for per-section attention. Process in full when cross-references matter, chunk when sections are independent and you want each one analyzed thoroughly.

blocks.text: Look What You've Built!
You've now worked across every major Claude surface:

• Chat with Connectors, reasoning modes, skills, memory, and Artifacts
  • Claude Code
  • Claude Cowork
  • Claude Design
  • Claude for Small Business
And you've learned the meta-skills that make them work together: workflow design, multi-tool execution, and now long-document mastery.

That's the full toolkit! The work from here is bringing it to your own projects — the contracts you're about to sign, the launches you're planning, the analyses you've been putting off, the work that's been waiting for a better tool. 

You have everything you need, now go build something ambitious! Good luck!

content.value: The Attention Drift Problem

Three contradictions found across nearly a hundred pages. But before you trust this output completely, there's one risk worth knowing about: attention drift.
